prompt: Write a novel about a teenage heroine who grows up and ends up changing the world

outline.name: The Last Lake
outline.description: Introduce sixteen-year-old Nia Vale, her family, and Saint Orra, a city organized around a shrinking, polluted reservoir. Nia secretly maps illegal neighborhood pipes to help families in Cinder Row obtain water beyond their official credits. Her mother Amara repairs Meridian filtration towers, while Nia's younger brother Tavi struggles with a respiratory illness requiring clean water. Nia's friendship with courier Jo Saye reveals their contrasting beliefs: Nia trusts data and systems, while Jo insists that collective action matters more than evidence alone. The chapter establishes Meridian's algorithmic rule, the city's class divisions, and Nia's determination to expose what she believes is a correctable technical failure.

outline.name: The Hidden Schedule
outline.description: Nia notices that wealthy districts receive uninterrupted water even during emergency cutoffs imposed on poorer neighborhoods. She compares household schedules, reservoir levels, and maintenance records, discovering patterns that contradict Meridian's public explanations. With Jo's reluctant assistance, she uses her mechanical skill to repair and access a damaged maintenance drone, naming it Morrow. The drone retrieves fragments of internal routing data suggesting that water is being diverted outside the city. Nia becomes convinced that the Allocation Engine is concealing deliberate political choices. Amara warns her not to mistake suspicion for proof, but Nia decides that obtaining the complete records is worth the risk.

outline.name: Morrow's Memory
outline.description: Nia and Jo investigate abandoned pumping infrastructure while Morrow reconstructs corrupted files. They uncover evidence of a concealed pipeline carrying reservoir water toward wealthy coastal enclaves and private desalination reserves. More alarming sensor data indicates toxic runoff entering the northern watershed from Helix Meridian's lithium and rare-earth mines. Nia learns that Helix has a contract with Meridian to build a privatized desalination complex once the reservoir is declared irrecoverable. She sees the shape of a manufactured crisis but struggles to explain the evidence without exposing her mother and neighbors. Jo urges her to build allies before releasing anything; Nia instead prepares a broadcast under her own control.

outline.name: The Broadcast Wall
outline.description: Nia and Jo project maps, routing records, and sensor readings across the walls of Cinder Row. The revelations spark neighborhood meetings, anger, and the first public protests against Meridian. Some residents are inspired, while others fear that Nia's accusations will bring retaliation. Meridian responds with a polished countercampaign claiming the maps are fabricated and that unauthorized pipes caused the shortages. Nia's certainty hardens into defiance when technicians quietly confirm that some of her data is genuine. During a raid on her home and Amara's workplace, Amara refuses to certify falsified filtration reports. She is arrested for sabotage, Tavi's medical allocation is revoked, and Nia flees with Morrow and the surviving records.

outline.name: Under the Reservoir
outline.description: Nia and Jo escape Saint Orra through disused irrigation tunnels beneath the reservoir basin. The journey exposes the physical consequences of Meridian's policies: abandoned districts, contaminated pools, and families moving through the dark with stolen containers. Nia wants to return for Tavi and Amara, but Jo persuades her that the records must survive. They emerge into the dry agricultural belt and are taken in by Farid Anwar, a farmer whose land has been damaged by mining runoff. Farid introduces them to the Open Current, a loose network of organizers, engineers, displaced families, and young couriers. Nia expects the network to help her reveal the truth, but immediately clashes with its distrust of centralized leadership.

outline.name: Open Current
outline.description: Nia meets the Open Current's principal members: refugee radio operator Lio Chen, hydrologist Dr. Sera Okafor, and former municipal engineer Tomas Vale, Nia's estranged uncle. The group debates whether to prioritize public exposure, direct sabotage, emergency water delivery, or watershed restoration. Rural members resent city activists who treat farms as symbols, while refugees fear that both sides will abandon them when supplies diminish. Nia withholds some of the stolen records and proposes a single coordinated operation based on her calculations. Her brilliance impresses several younger members, but Jo recognizes that Nia is already trying to make the network dependent on her.

outline.name: The Wrong Calculation
outline.description: Nia takes control of an emergency water shipment and secretly redirects it according to her model of maximum social benefit. The decision sends water away from Farid's settlement toward a larger population center, leaving a seed bank unprotected during a heat wave. Crops fail, and years of agricultural work are lost. Farid confronts Nia publicly, arguing that she treated people as variables rather than partners. The Open Current fractures, with some members demanding that Nia be expelled and others defending her intentions. Nia discovers that key records needed to prove the Helix conspiracy were destroyed, meaning her evidence can be dismissed as incomplete. For the first time, she realizes that being right may not be enough.

outline.name: Many Witnesses
outline.description: Sera challenges Nia to rebuild the case through independently verifiable evidence rather than a single stolen archive. The Open Current establishes community-owned sensor stations in farms, refugee camps, and city neighborhoods. Residents learn to inspect the data, dispute readings, and add testimony about contamination and water diversions. Nia initially resists surrendering control of the network, fearing sabotage and misinformation, but Jo forces her to confront the resemblance between her methods and Meridian's closed system. Farid agrees to help if the project supports watershed recovery rather than only political exposure. Nia begins repairing relationships by listening to people whose needs contradict her preferred plan.

outline.name: The Living Map
outline.description: The Open Current turns from evidence gathering to practical survival. Engineers repair old canals, communities restore wetlands, and local assemblies decide how to divide scarce water among farms, refugees, and urban neighborhoods. Nia designs an open mapping platform that makes every allocation visible and revisable. Her work is now collaborative rather than secretive, and she learns to accept corrections from people with less technical training but deeper local knowledge. Morrow becomes a symbol of shared stewardship instead of Nia's private tool. Meanwhile, intercepted messages reveal that Helix agents are planning to destroy the wetland sites and blame the attack on the Open Current.

outline.name: The Price of Proof
outline.description: Meridian escalates repression by cutting power to rebellious districts, arresting organizers, and broadcasting claims that the Open Current is a terrorist movement. Helix agents sabotage restoration sites, and Farid is killed after refusing to sell his land. His death devastates Nia and exposes the cost of treating truth as a shield against violence. Amara is transferred to a remote detention facility, while Tavi's health worsens. Some members demand a centralized emergency command under Nia, believing only speed can save them. Nia is tempted to accept, but Jo and Sera remind her that a movement built around one gifted leader would reproduce the old system and collapse if that leader were captured.

outline.name: The Mesh
outline.description: Lio helps Nia transform Morrow's damaged transmitter into a mesh-broadcast system linking thousands of small independent stations. The network distributes sensor readings, repair instructions, witness testimony, and local decisions without relying on Meridian's communication grid. Nia broadcasts a carefully documented account of the diversions and contamination, but the broadcast becomes powerful only when ordinary people compare their own data and confirm the pattern. Meridian technicians leak the Allocation Engine's source code, revealing that political priorities were hidden inside supposedly neutral calculations. Workers in the coastal enclaves disclose the private pipelines, and families in Saint Orra begin opening illegal connections to displaced communities. Nia understands that her role is not to speak for everyone, but to help everyone speak to one another.

outline.name: The Dry Siege
outline.description: The revelations trigger mass strikes, coordinated occupations of pumping stations, and a wave of civil disobedience across Saint Orra and the agricultural belt. Meridian attempts a final crackdown by shutting down the main filtration towers, gambling that thirst will restore obedience. Nia and the Open Current must coordinate a response without becoming a command hierarchy. Inside detention, Amara works with imprisoned technicians to interrupt the shutdown sequence. Tavi, despite his fragile health, helps organize emergency clinics and supply routes, showing Nia that care work is part of political resistance. Morrow's network begins failing under the strain, forcing Nia to trust local operators and relinquish direct control.

outline.name: The Towers Hold
outline.description: As filtration systems fail and violence threatens to spread, Amara sabotages Meridian's shutdown from inside, keeping the towers operating long enough for Open Current engineers to seize them. Nia coordinates public assemblies rather than issuing unilateral orders, allowing neighborhoods to choose priorities and report their needs. Meridian security forces lose cohesion when technicians, patrol officers, and municipal workers refuse to enforce impossible directives. Helix executives attempt to flee with financial records and water contracts, but leaked evidence exposes their role. The Authority collapses, though the victory is chaotic: reservoirs remain poisoned, essential districts are unsafe, and no one possesses a complete plan for what comes next.

outline.name: After the Fall
outline.description: In the aftermath, Nia becomes an international symbol of the uprising while Saint Orra confronts the limits of victory. Helix officials flee or reinvent themselves as reformers, trials begin, and rival factions argue over whether the old infrastructure should be nationalized or dismantled. The reservoir cannot be restored, so whole neighborhoods must be abandoned through a painful managed retreat. Nia's family loses its home in Cinder Row; Amara survives but cannot return to tower work, and Tavi remains ill. Nia helps establish elected Water Councils, transparent data trusts, community treatment plants, and legal protections defining water as a shared public right. She refuses a formal executive role, though many supporters accuse her of abandoning the movement.

outline.name: The Commons Assembly
outline.description: Years later, an adult Nia oversees the first global Water Commons Assembly. Nations facing their own water crises propose replacing Meridian's monopoly with a powerful centralized authority, arguing that only unified control can prevent future collapse. Nia recognizes the old logic beneath the new language and remembers her younger self's belief that justice depended on possessing the complete answer. She advocates a distributed system of local councils, public scientists, farmers, workers, and displaced communities, with open records and mechanisms for constant revision. The resolution is imperfect and fiercely contested, but it establishes a living global commons rather than a new monopoly. Watching young delegates take responsibility for decisions she once would have claimed alone, Nia understands that changing the world means creating structures through which people can continue repairing it together.

chapters.content:
# The Last Lake

At six in the morning, Saint Orra was already thirsty.

The city woke to the click of meters refusing water. In Cinder Row, taps coughed air, then a brown thread that smelled of pennies and wet stone. Above the eastern wall, where the reservoir should have shone silver, the Last Lake lay under a skin of green scum. Its exposed banks ringed the water like old scars. Towers rose beyond it, white and needle-thin, drawing the remaining clean water through Meridian’s filters and sending it downhill—to wherever the Allocation Engine decided it was needed most.

Nia Vale knew the Engine’s explanation by heart.

**Distribution is not deprivation. Distribution is balance.**

The words glowed on every public screen as she crossed the roof of Building 19 with a coil of blue tubing over one shoulder. Her school uniform was hidden beneath a gray work jacket, and her braids were tucked into a cap. Sixteen years old, narrow-shouldered, and quick enough to move between the solar panels without making them rattle, she looked like a maintenance apprentice if anyone happened to glance up.

No one glanced up. People in Cinder Row had learned to keep their eyes on the nearest meter.

Nia crouched beside a rusted vent and unrolled her map. It was not a map of streets. It was a map of thirst: apartment blocks marked in red, public taps in yellow, and a branching network of illegal pipes drawn in blue pencil. The pipes had been installed over years by residents who had run out of credits and patience. Most were leaky, badly joined, and dangerous. They were also the only reason several families on the top floors had water after Meridian’s morning cutoff.

She clipped the tubing to a valve she had fitted two nights ago. A soft shudder traveled through the line. Somewhere below, a cistern began to fill.

“Hold,” she whispered, watching the pressure gauge. “Hold, hold—”

The needle steadied in the green.

A cheer rose faintly from the courtyard. Nia smiled, but only for a second. The pipe would serve twelve apartments for three hours, perhaps four, before someone reported the pressure anomaly. She marked the time, flow rate, and valve position in a waterproof notebook. Data mattered. Data remembered what people were too tired to remember.

A pebble struck the vent beside her.

“You’re going to get caught because you write down your crimes,” Jo Saye called from the next roof.

Jo stood with one foot on a chimney and a courier’s orange satchel strapped across her chest. Her black curls had escaped their scarf, and her grin suggested she had been waiting for this exact moment. She was the same age as Nia, though she carried herself like someone who had already been disappointed by three governments.

“They’re not crimes,” Nia said.

“Tell that to Meridian’s patrol drones.”

“Tell Meridian to provide the water it promised.”

Jo leaped the gap between buildings. She landed badly, windmilled her arms, and caught herself on a pipe.

Nia reached for her. “Idiot.”

“Accurate, but unhelpful.” Jo recovered and peered at the notebook. “How many households?”

“Twelve here. Twenty-six through the laundry conduit. Fourteen in Block Twenty-One if the old pressure gate still works.”

“You count families like you count screws.”

“I count what can be measured.”

“And what can’t?”

Nia capped her pen. “Doesn’t become more real because you give it a speech.”

Jo’s smile faded. Below them, a woman hurried from a tap carrying two empty jugs. The screen on the corner announced that Cinder Row had exceeded its equitable consumption threshold. Across the reservoir, the terraces of Aurelia Heights glittered behind glass walls. Their fountains ran in thin, continuous ribbons, ornamental and blue.

Jo pointed. “Can your numbers explain that?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Explain.”

“Different elevation zones. Different infrastructure age. Different emergency classifications.” Nia tapped her temple. “The Engine prioritizes hospitals, fire suppression, and high-density residential nodes.”

“Aurelia has three hospitals and six swimming clubs.”

“Then the model is weighting something else.”

“Or someone is telling it to.”

Nia folded the map. The thought had visited her before, unwelcome and persistent. The Allocation Engine was supposed to be impartial: a lattice of sensors, forecasts, and rules built after the old water wars. It calculated reservoir levels, rainfall probabilities, household credits, industrial demand, and contamination risk. No official could simply decide who drank. No neighbor could demand a favor. The system made the city safe from human selfishness.

That was what Amara always said, though lately she said it without conviction.

A cough echoed from the stairwell below. Nia froze.

“Tavi?”

She dropped the tubing and ran.

Her brother was sitting halfway down the stairs, one hand braced against the wall. He was nine, small for his age, with a copper inhaler clenched in the other hand. His breaths came in shallow clicks. The air in Cinder Row carried dust from the dry lakebed, and the dust had been settling in his lungs for months.

Nia knelt. “Did you take the morning dose?”

He nodded, then coughed again.

“Water?”

“Mom said not until she gets home.”

“Mom says a lot of things when she’s scared.”

Tavi gave her a look that was far too knowing for nine. “Is she scared?”

Nia helped him stand. “She repairs filtration towers. She’s scared of faulty relays, corroded membranes, and supervisors who think a warning light is an insult. Not this.”

It was a lie. Amara had left before dawn for Tower Fourteen, kissing Tavi’s hair and checking his water credit twice. The credit was almost gone. His treatment required distilled water for the vaporizer, and Meridian had classified his illness as chronic but non-emergency. The classification meant the machine could wait.

Their apartment smelled of boiled cloth and machine oil. Amara’s tools occupied half the kitchen table, each laid out in a precise row. Nia poured from the hidden jug beneath the sink, then stopped when the level fell below the line she had drawn.

Tavi noticed. “That’s for Mom.”

“It’s for all of us.”

“You said data matters.”

“Data is not the same as surrender.”

She filled the vaporizer. Tavi leaned toward the warm mist, shoulders gradually loosening. Nia watched his face until the blue tinge left his lips.

On the wall screen, Meridian’s morning bulletin began. A calm voice reported reservoir stabilization, responsible household conservation, and the successful activation of a new private reclamation contract. Behind the announcer, a graphic showed the Last Lake as a bright blue oval. Nia could see the real reservoir through the window: green, shrunken, and ringed with abandoned docks.

At noon, Amara came home in a stained tower suit. She moved carefully, as if every joint had been tightened one turn too far. Nia saw the black smear beneath her fingernails and the fresh burn at her wrist.

“What happened?” Nia asked.

“Relay housing cracked.” Amara set her helmet down. “Nothing serious.”

“Did you file a fault report?”

“Of course.”

“Was Tower Fourteen drawing above its allocation?”

Amara looked at her. “Why?”

“Because Block 19 lost pressure while the tower flushed.”

“The Engine schedules flushes.”

“Then the Engine scheduled a neighborhood cutoff during a tower cycle.”

“Perhaps.” Amara washed her hands in a cup, not under the tap. “Nia, a pattern is not a conspiracy.”

“I didn’t say conspiracy.”

“You’re thinking it loudly.”

Jo appeared in the doorway with two ration buns and an expression that meant she had already heard enough. “She’s thinking the city has a leak.”

“Everything has a leak,” Amara said. “The question is whether you can survive finding it.”

Nia spread her notebook on the table. Pressure readings. Cutoff times. Pipe routes. Reservoir levels copied from public displays. The numbers did not fit. Cinder Row lost water whenever the towers reported emergency conservation, but Aurelia Heights did not. The difference was not random. It repeated every six days.

Amara studied the pages in silence.

“Who else knows?” she asked.

“No one.”

Jo lifted a bun. “I know.”

“Jo,” Amara said, “knowing is not the same as helping.”

Jo’s eyes flicked to Nia. “That’s what I keep telling her.”

Nia gathered the papers. “If the Engine is wrong, the fault can be corrected.”

“And if the people running it like the result?” Jo asked.

Nia looked toward the lake. A gull circled above the poisoned water and vanished into the glare.

“Then I’ll find the error they’re hiding,” she said.

Jo shook her head. “You still think proof makes people move.”

“No. Proof makes it impossible for them to pretend they’re standing still.”

Outside, somewhere beneath the street, the illegal pipe knocked once, twice, then began to flow. In twelve apartments, families lifted their containers. In the towers, Meridian’s lights continued their measured blinking. And beneath the city’s official map, Nia drew another blue line.

chapters.name: The Hidden Schedule
chapters.content:
# The Hidden Schedule

By the next morning, the city had changed its explanation.

Cinder Row’s taps remained dry, but the public screens no longer said the district had exceeded its equitable threshold. They said an emergency pressure event had required temporary isolation. Temporary, Nia noted, meant six hours on the screen and eleven hours in the pipes.

She copied the notice into her notebook before breakfast. Then she copied the reservoir reading beneath it: 18.7 percent capacity, down from 18.9 the night before. The numbers were small, but the lake did not lose water in neat, invisible increments. Every decrease had a source. Every source had a destination.

Tavi slept beside the vaporizer, his face turned toward its warm breath. Amara had left a cup of distilled water measured to the line and a note beside it.

**For his treatment. Do not use.**

Nia stared at the sentence until it became a command addressed to someone else. Then she tucked the cup farther from the edge of the table and went to school.

She did not listen to the history lecture. Instead, she used the classroom terminal during independent study, entering household schedules copied from neighbors’ meters and the maintenance bulletins Amara had brought home over the years. Meridian published repairs in broad categories—membrane cleaning, pressure balancing, contamination response—but the tower crews worked by narrower schedules. Tower Fourteen flushed on the second and eighth days of each cycle. Tower Nine, serving Aurelia Heights, flushed on the same nights.

Yet Cinder Row lost water during both cycles. Aurelia lost none.

Nia overlaid the schedules with reservoir levels, rainfall forecasts, and the city’s emergency classifications. She checked her calculations three times. A conservation cutoff should have followed a drop in the lake or a contamination alert. Instead, the cutoff came when the reservoir was stable and vanished just before Aurelia’s evening demand rose.

The pattern was not a six-day discrepancy anymore. It was a six-day decision.

At lunch, Jo found her behind the bicycle sheds, where the school’s collection pipes made a convenient curtain of noise.

“You have the expression,” Jo said, handing her half a ration bun.

“What expression?”

“The one that means you’ve replaced sleep with arithmetic.”

Nia showed her the screen. “Look at the district schedules.”

Jo chewed, squinting. “Aurelia’s pressure stays constant.”

“During emergency isolation.”

“Maybe their pipes are better.”

“Their towers draw from the same reservoir. The public explanation says the cutoff protects the whole system.”

“And your explanation?”

“Someone is routing water around the cutoff.”

Jo swallowed. “Someone with access to a routing system.”

“Or the Engine is doing it.”

“Engines don’t want things.”

“People program priorities.”

“That’s not the same as proving they changed them.” Jo leaned back against the wall. “What do you want me to do?”

“Help me get maintenance records.”

Jo laughed once. “You mean steal them.”

“I mean access them.”

“Those words are cousins who don’t visit the same neighborhoods.”

That afternoon, they searched the municipal repair yard. Jo knew which fences had broken alarms and which guards accepted a courier’s wave without looking up. Behind a stack of retired filter housings, Nia found the drone.

It was the size of a bread box, its white shell blackened by grit. One rotor was missing, and a red service light blinked beneath a cracked lens. The stamped designation read **M-ORR/7**, though half the letters had been scraped away.

“Absolutely not,” Jo said.

Nia knelt beside it. “It’s a maintenance scout.”

“It’s dead.”

“Damaged.”

“It has a hole where its eye belongs.”

“That’s a lens, not an eye.”

Jo folded her arms. “You’re going to repair it.”

“I’m going to see whether it can be repaired.”

They carried the drone into an abandoned pump shed. Nia scavenged a rotor from a survey toy, soldered a bridge across the power board, and cleaned grit from the memory slot with a strip torn from Jo’s courier receipt. The drone shuddered twice, rose three centimeters, and struck the ceiling.

Jo caught it against her chest. “It hates us.”

“It has no emotional architecture.”

“It has excellent instincts.”

Nia replaced the cracked lens with a piece of polished bottle glass. The machine woke again. A line of pale green text crawled across its internal display.

**MAINTENANCE UNIT M-ORR/7. MEMORY PARTITION FAILURE.**

“Morrow,” Nia said.

Jo looked at her. “You named it?”

“Designation was inconvenient.”

“You named the stolen municipal drone.”

“It’s not stolen yet.”

Morrow lifted itself on its three functioning rotors. Its camera turned toward the shed door, then toward Nia’s notebook, as if learning what mattered. Nia connected her tablet to its service port. Most of the files were corrupted: pressure maps reduced to bands of color, inspection logs filled with broken symbols, coordinates that repeated the same impossible decimal.

Then one fragment opened.

**ROUTE CLASS: EXTERNAL RESERVE. DESTINATION:—**

The rest dissolved into static.

Nia’s pulse beat hard against her throat. “External reserve.”

“Could be a reserve outside the district,” Jo said. “A hospital. Fire control.”

“Then why hide the destination?”

“Maybe because the file is damaged.”

Nia enlarged the route trace. A line left the reservoir’s eastern basin, passed beneath the industrial belt, and continued toward the coast. It did not connect to any public district node.

Morrow gave a thin electronic chirp. Another fragment appeared.

**TRANSFER WINDOW: 02:10–02:40. PRIORITY—**

The words ended there, but Nia already knew what happened at 2:10. Her neighbors’ meters stopped. Aurelia Heights’ fountains brightened.

They took Morrow home under Jo’s courier cloak. Amara was at the kitchen table, repairing the strap of her tower helmet. She looked from the drone to Nia, then to Jo.

“No,” she said.

“You haven’t heard—”

“I know that face too.” Amara set down the needle. “You found something, and now you’ve decided danger is evidence of importance.”

Nia placed the tablet on the table. “The routing data shows water leaving the reservoir during Cinder Row’s cutoffs.”

“Shows fragments.”

“Fragments that match the schedules.”

“Matching is not proof.”

Nia felt heat climb her neck. “You always say that when the proof is inconvenient.”

Amara’s expression tightened. “I say it because Meridian can take a partial record, call it sabotage, and put you in a cell before anyone hears the rest.”

For a moment, the only sound was Tavi’s vaporizer ticking.

Amara reached across the table and touched the burn on her wrist. “Tower crews are told not to question allocation orders. We report faults. The Engine decides. If you are wrong, you expose us for nothing. If you are right, they will not thank you for correcting them.”

Nia looked at Tavi. His water cup stood untouched, exactly at the marked line. She thought of the eastern route disappearing under the city while her brother measured each breath.

“I need the complete records,” she said.

Jo closed her eyes. “There it is.”

Amara heard the decision in Nia’s voice. “What are you planning?”

“To find where Morrow was assigned before it was discarded.”

“That is not a plan. That is a door.”

“Then I’ll find the key.”

Outside, the neighborhood meters clicked in unison. On the public screen, Meridian announced another temporary pressure event. Across the reservoir, Aurelia Heights remained bright.

Morrow’s damaged camera turned toward the window. In its cracked glass, the city appeared divided into two schedules: one written for those who waited, and another for those who were never asked to.

chapters.name: Morrow's Memory
chapters.content:
# Morrow's Memory

Morrow remembered in pieces.

For three nights it sat inside the kitchen cupboard beneath a stack of clean bowls, its three rotors removed and arranged on a towel. Nia fed it power from a salvaged converter while Tavi slept and Amara worked the late shift at Tower Fourteen. Each time the drone woke, its camera clicked toward her, then a string of damaged symbols crawled across the tablet.

“Try the old partition,” Jo said on the fourth night.

She was crouched beside the window, listening for patrol engines. Rain tapped the glass, though the forecast had promised clear air. In Saint Orra, even weather announcements had become suggestions.

“The old partition is the damaged partition,” Nia said.

“Then damage it differently.”

Nia glanced at her. “That is not a technical method.”

“It is a courier method. If a door won’t open, stop treating it like a door.”

Nia almost objected. Then she remembered how Morrow’s service files had been indexed: not by date, but by assignment code. She searched for the drone’s serial number, found a buried maintenance tag, and ran the tag through a discarded municipal diagnostic program.

The screen filled with blue lines.

Morrow’s last assignment had not been Tower Fourteen, or any tower in Cinder Row. It had been **BASIN EAST—PUMP ARRAY 3**, a facility marked inactive six years earlier.

Jo leaned closer. “Inactive means abandoned.”

“Or removed from the public map.”

“Those are not the same thing?”

“Not in Meridian language.”

They left before dawn, when the city’s patrols changed shifts and the pipe network slept between pressure cycles. Jo carried her orange satchel; Nia carried Morrow beneath a mechanic’s tarp. They crossed the industrial belt by way of drainage alleys, stepping over salt-crusted cables and puddles that shimmered with oil. The air smelled of metal and wet dust.

Pump Array 3 stood beyond a collapsed freight viaduct. Its concrete walls leaned inward, crowded by thorn trees and coils of dead tubing. A Meridian seal had been painted over the entrance, but the old letters remained visible beneath it.

Nia placed her palm against the lock. “There’s power.”

“Of course there is,” Jo said. “Abandoned places are always the most expensive to maintain.”

Morrow rose from beneath the tarp. Its replacement lens caught the gray morning. It flew toward the service panel and projected a narrow beam across the rusted plate. The lock clicked.

Inside, the pump hall was cold enough to tighten Nia’s lungs. Catwalks crossed a pit full of silent machinery. Dust lay thick on the rails, but a clean track ran along the floor, as if something heavy had been dragged recently.

They found the first pipe behind a false wall.

It was not municipal blue. It was black composite, wider than Nia’s body, wrapped in fresh insulation. A pressure gauge pulsed steadily beside it.

Jo touched the needle with one finger. “That’s moving.”

Nia opened her notebook and copied the reading. “The reservoir is supposedly under emergency conservation.”

“Maybe the pipe is conserving it somewhere else.”

Morrow gave a sharp chirp. Its camera turned toward a ladder descending beneath the pump hall.

The lower chamber held an array of sensors. Some had been smashed. Others still glowed, recording temperature, conductivity, and chemical traces in the water flowing through the pipe. Nia connected Morrow to the nearest terminal. A file opened with a date from two months earlier.

**DESTINATION CLASS: COASTAL PRIVATE RESERVE.**

Below it, a route diagram showed the black pipe leaving the eastern basin, crossing beneath the industrial belt, and splitting at the coast. One branch ended at a sealed desalination reserve labeled with a Helix Meridian emblem. The other fed three compounds whose names Nia recognized from city news: Pelagos Crown, Whitehaven Reach, and North Glass.

Wealthy coastal enclaves. Places with private weather domes, greenhouses, and swimming pools advertised as climate refuges.

Jo’s face went still. “They’re filling private tanks with reservoir water.”

“Not just tanks.” Nia enlarged the records. “The reserve is being built before the lake is declared irrecoverable.”

A second file contained construction estimates. A third showed projected tariffs: household access sold by subscription, medical water billed separately, agricultural water restricted to licensed producers.

At the bottom of the contract, two names appeared together: **MERIDIAN AUTHORITY** and **HELIX MERIDIAN RESOURCE GROUP**.

Nia read the line twice. “Helix is financing the desalination complex.”

“After the lake dies.”

“After Meridian says it dies.”

Jo looked at her. “That’s a different sentence.”

“It is the whole sentence.”

Morrow’s memory stuttered. The display went black, then flashed a map of the northern watershed. Red marks appeared along the tributaries above Saint Orra. Nia recognized the basin from school maps: the snowmelt channels, the villages, the reed marshes that filtered water before it reached the reservoir.

Sensor readings poured across the screen. Lithium. Arsenic. Rare-earth solvent. The concentrations rose sharply downstream from a series of open-pit mines operated by Helix Meridian.

For several seconds, Nia could hear nothing but the low pulse of the concealed pipe.

“Those levels would poison the reservoir,” she said.

“Eventually?”

“Already.” She scrolled through the timestamps. “The runoff begins during storm releases. The public contamination alerts only list household discharge.”

Jo’s jaw tightened. “So they drain the clean water to the coast and poison what remains.”

Nia wanted to say no. She wanted a broken sensor, a mislabeled file, any flaw that would turn the shape in front of her back into an accident. But the dates aligned with the cutoffs. The mine releases aligned with the algae blooms. The construction contract began six months before Meridian’s first irrecoverable-reservoir forecast.

A manufactured crisis did not look like a villain standing beneath a black flag. It looked like separate departments following reasonable procedures.

The terminal chimed. A warning appeared: **REMOTE PURGE REQUEST RECEIVED.**

“Someone knows,” Jo said.

Nia pulled the cable free. Morrow jerked upward, and a shower of sparks fell from the terminal.

Footsteps sounded above them.

They ran. Jo reached the ladder first and kicked a loose wrench through the stairwell. It clanged across the catwalk. A voice shouted from the entrance. Nia shoved Morrow into her coat, and they climbed through a side hatch into the thorn trees as boots struck the pump hall floor.

They did not stop until the viaduct hid them from the facility.

Back at the apartment, Nia copied everything onto three memory wafers. One she hid inside the valve housing beneath the kitchen sink. One she sealed in the lining of Jo’s satchel. The third stayed in her hand.

Amara came home with a bandage around her wrist and stopped when she saw the maps spread across the table.

“What happened?”

“Nothing,” Nia said too quickly.

Amara looked at the red tributaries, the coastal route, the Helix seal. “That is not nothing.”

Nia’s mouth went dry. She could explain the data. She could explain the timestamps, the contract, the sensor calibration. But every explanation led back to the pump array, the illegal pipe network, Morrow, and the people whose names were written in her notebook. If she broadcast the records and Meridian traced them, Cinder Row would become evidence too.

Tavi coughed in his sleep. Amara crossed to him, checking the vaporizer, and Nia saw how carefully her mother hid the fear in her hands.

“Who else knows?” Amara asked.

“Jo.”

“Then tell more people.”

Nia looked up. “Why?”

“Because one frightened person can be silenced. Two can be arrested. A neighborhood can remember.”

Jo, sitting by the door, nodded. “We need allies before we release this.”

“We need the records out before they purge them.”

“Both can be true.”

Nia turned to the tablet. The city’s broadcast grid offered an access window at midnight. She could splice the maps into the public emergency channel, show the pipeline, the mines, the contract. No committee could dilute the facts. No frightened neighbor could decide they were too dangerous.

Jo stood. “You’re planning to do it alone.”

“I’m planning to make sure it happens.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

Nia inserted the third wafer. Morrow’s damaged camera fixed on her, its bottle-glass eye reflecting the red watershed and the bright coastal enclaves.

“I have spent weeks proving the pattern,” Nia said. “If I wait for everyone to agree, Meridian will erase it.”

Jo’s voice softened. “If you speak without them, Meridian will call it your story.”

Nia opened a new broadcast file and began arranging the evidence in sequence: cutoff, diversion, runoff, contract. A story, she thought, was only a pattern people could see.

Outside, Cinder Row’s taps coughed air. Far across the dark city, the coastal domes glowed like captive moons.

Nia named the file **THE WATER THEY STOLE** and set it to transmit at midnight.

chapters.name: The Broadcast Wall
chapters.content:
# The Broadcast Wall

At eleven fifty-eight, Nia changed the broadcast plan.

She had meant to send the evidence through Meridian’s emergency grid, a clean sequence of maps and readings that would appear on every licensed screen in Saint Orra. But Jo returned from the stairwell with three neighbors behind her and said, “The grid is watched.”

“Everything is watched.”

“Then let them watch the walls.”

They carried the projector to the courtyard between the apartment blocks. Jo had borrowed it from the laundry cooperative, where its usual purpose was displaying repair instructions. Nia connected Morrow’s transmitter, fed the maps through a cracked maintenance tablet, and aimed the lens at the broad concrete wall above the communal taps.

The first image appeared as a pale blue rectangle: Cinder Row’s cutoff schedule, overlaid on the reservoir levels.

People came out slowly. They arrived in slippers, work coats, carrying cups and empty containers. Tavi watched from the apartment window, his forehead pressed to the glass beside the vaporizer’s curling mist. Amara stood beneath him with one hand raised, a warning or a blessing; Nia could not tell which.

Jo tapped the projector housing. “Show them something they know.”

Nia displayed the six-day pattern. Red bars marked the hours when Cinder Row went dry. A gold line showed Aurelia Heights receiving uninterrupted flow.

A woman near the taps laughed once, without humor. “They told us the pressure was unstable.”

“Pressure doesn’t know district borders,” said the old man from Block Nine.

“It does if Meridian programs it to,” someone answered.

Nia advanced the map. The concealed pipeline drew itself across the wall, leaving the eastern basin and running toward the coast. At its end, private reserves glowed white beneath the names Pelagos Crown, Whitehaven Reach, and North Glass.

For a moment no one spoke. Then a boy threw his empty cup at the wall.

The cup struck the image of a swimming pool.

“They have pools?” a woman shouted.

“They have gardens,” said another. “My daughter drinks recycled steam.”

Nia showed the sensor readings next: lithium, arsenic, rare-earth solvent, rising downstream from Helix mines. She enlarged the timestamps until the numbers filled the wall. Finally, the Meridian-Helix contract appeared, with the privatized desalination complex and its household tariffs.

The crowd changed as the evidence accumulated. Anger moved through it like pressure in a pipe, gathering wherever there was a weakness. People called relatives. Someone began copying the files onto old phones. A mechanic from Tower Eleven stood on a crate and asked Nia to repeat the sensor calibration. A teacher demanded to know why the public contamination notices named household discharge but not the mines.

Nia answered until her throat hurt.

The answers did not calm anyone. They gave the anger direction.

By dawn, the courtyard had become a meeting. Residents formed circles beneath the projected maps. They argued over whether to block the district valve, whether the illegal blue-tubing lines should be opened wider, whether Meridian patrols could be resisted with tools and fire extinguishers. Some wanted to march to the municipal offices. Others wanted to hide their children and wait for the authorities to tire.

A woman named Salma caught Nia by the sleeve. “You have proof?”

“I have records.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

Nia looked at the wall, where the red watershed marks flickered under the projector’s heat. “The files are authentic.”

“Authentic is not the same as safe.” Salma glanced toward the street. “You put our pipes on that wall.”

“I obscured the household addresses.”

“Meridian doesn’t need addresses. It needs a reason.”

The reason arrived before noon.

Every public screen in Saint Orra switched from weather forecasts to the calm face of Director Pell, Meridian’s communications chief. Behind her stood an image of a blue reservoir and a row of smiling children holding silver cups.

“Unauthorized maps circulating in Cinder Row,” Pell said, “are fabricated composites produced by vandals seeking to destabilize essential services. Illegal neighborhood pipes have caused pressure loss, contamination, and dangerous backflow. Meridian urges residents not to assist saboteurs.”

The statement was polished enough to feel rehearsed before Nia had finished speaking. Meridian released diagrams showing blue lines branching wildly through Cinder Row, each labeled *unregulated theft*. It released a second video of a Helix mine, clean and sunlit, its workers wearing white masks while a voice explained responsible extraction.

By evening, patrols had placed warning notices over the courtyard walls. A city broadcaster called Nia an anonymous teenage extremist. Anonymous, she thought, while half the neighborhood knew her name.

Jo found her in the maintenance room, where the projector hummed beside a stack of water crates.

“They’re scared,” Jo said.

“Good.”

“They’re angry.”

“Better.”

“They’re also saying the pipe network caused everything.”

Nia turned sharply. “It supplies twelve buildings. The diversions carry millions of liters.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you repeating them?”

“I’m telling you what people are hearing.” Jo folded her arms. “If you only listen to evidence that agrees with you, you become Meridian with better intentions.”

The words landed harder than Nia expected. She looked down at the tablet, where the contract’s signature blocks remained frozen beneath a red warning banner.

At that moment, two figures entered through the rear door. They wore gray Meridian maintenance uniforms, but one had removed her identification strip.

“We work at Tower Nine,” the woman said. “The records on your wall are real. Not all of them, but the routing code is. We’ve seen that destination class.”

Her companion nodded. “And those cutoff cycles match the flush schedule. We were ordered to alter the public logs.”

“Will you testify?” Nia asked.

The woman’s eyes moved to the water crates. “Not with my face attached.”

“Then the data still has to speak.”

“No,” Jo said quietly. “People have to speak. Data can be buried.”

Nia wanted to argue. Instead, she copied the technicians’ statements onto a fourth file and asked their names. They gave only first names, Iven and Rusk, then left by separate doors.

That night, the raid began at Tower Fourteen.

Amara was repairing a fouled intake valve when security officers entered the control room. They carried a digital order accusing her of sabotaging filtration by falsifying maintenance checks. On the central screen, a report waited for her certification. It stated that the tower’s failure had been caused by unauthorized neighborhood pipes and malicious sensor interference.

Amara read it once.

Then she set down her wrench.

“This is false.”

The supervisor’s expression did not change. “Certify it.”

“The intake levels are outside tolerance because the upstream water is contaminated.”

“Certify it.”

“Your report blames families for a condition recorded in the tower’s own sensors.”

The supervisor stepped closer. “You have a sick child, Amara Vale. Your medical allocation is conditional. Don’t confuse courage with carelessness.”

Amara’s bandaged wrist trembled. Her voice did not. “I won’t sign a lie.”

They arrested her for sabotage in front of the night crew.

At nearly the same time, Meridian officers broke the Vale apartment door. Nia woke to boots in the hall and Morrow’s warning chirp. Jo, who had stayed near the window, shoved the tablet beneath a floor mat. Amara was not there. Tavi sat up coughing as officers overturned the cupboards and tore the sink valve from its housing.

The wafer hidden there was gone before Nia could reach it.

“Where is the drone?” one officer demanded.

Morrow darted from behind the vaporizer. Nia caught it against her chest, taking a sharp edge across her palm. Jo kicked the room’s emergency light, plunging the apartment into darkness.

They ran through the laundry shaft while Tavi called for them.

Nia stopped at the lower landing. “We can’t leave him.”

Jo seized her shoulders. “If they catch you, the records disappear.”

“My mother—”

“Is already in their hands.”

A Meridian notice flashed across the hallway screen. **MEDICAL ALLOCATION: TAVI VALE—REVOKED PENDING INVESTIGATION.**

The words blurred. Nia heard her brother coughing above them, each breath thin and scraping.

Jo pulled the orange satchel from beneath her coat. “The wafer is here. The third is with you. We get out, preserve them, and come back with people.”

Nia pressed her bleeding hand around Morrow’s frame. “They took the sink copy.”

“Then two copies are still alive.”

Outside, alarms rolled through Cinder Row. Doors slammed. Someone shouted that patrols were sealing the avenue. Nia climbed through the laundry exit into an alley smelling of wet ash and hot circuitry. Behind her, the apartment windows glowed one by one as Meridian searched them.

She looked back only once. Tavi’s window was dark.

At the end of the alley, Jo led her toward the old freight tunnels, while Morrow limped through the air between them. Nia carried the tablet, the notebook, and the surviving records. She carried her mother’s refusal like a spark cupped in both hands.

The broadcast had not changed the city as she imagined. It had not made truth victorious. It had made truth dangerous to everyone who touched it.

Behind them, the projected wall still showed the red lines of the poisoned watershed. Patrol lights washed over the image, but could not erase the map from the concrete. People had seen it. People had copied it. Somewhere in Cinder Row, someone was already drawing it again.

Nia entered the tunnel.

Then the dark closed over Saint Orra.

chapters.name: Under the Reservoir
chapters.content:
## Under the Reservoir

The tunnel mouth was narrower than the map promised.

Nia turned sideways, pressed her injured palm against the concrete, and pulled herself through a gap where roots had broken the ceiling. Cold mud soaked one knee. Behind her, Jo whispered, “Move.”

“I’m moving.”

“Then move faster.”

Morrow gave a thin warning chirp between them. Its three working rotors twitched uselessly against the walls, and its bottle-glass lens caught the beam of Jo’s covered lamp. Nia reached back, dragged the drone by its frame, and felt something scrape her boot in the darkness.

Above them, Saint Orra was searching.

The raid sirens had faded, but Meridian’s patrols would be sealing the freight exits now. They would search apartments, clinics, tram depots, every place a frightened girl might carry a machine and two memory wafers. Nia could still see the look on Tavi’s face when she had left him behind: confusion first, then the terrible effort of pretending not to be afraid.

She stopped.

Jo collided with her shoulder. “What?”

“We go back.”

“No.”

“My brother is nine.”

“And your mother is in a detention truck. You can’t rescue either of them from a tunnel with half a battery and a bleeding hand.” Jo’s voice shook, though she kept it low. “If we go back, they get us too. Then the records disappear, and Meridian gets to call all of us liars.”

Nia looked at the wafer sealed inside the pocket against her ribs. The other was in Jo’s satchel. Two small black slivers, lighter than the copper inhaler Tavi carried everywhere. Their weight seemed obscene.

“I left him,” Nia said.

“You left a chance.” Jo caught her wrist. “Don’t turn that into abandoning him. We survive long enough to make a chance bigger.”

The old irrigation maps had shown a service route beneath the reservoir basin, built before Saint Orra’s towers and sealed when Meridian rerouted the city’s water. Nia had believed the tunnel would be empty. She had believed many things because empty spaces were easier to calculate.

It was not empty.

They found the first family near a collapsed junction: a woman, two boys, and an old man crouched around six stolen containers. The containers were marked with Aurelia Heights’ blue crescent, but their labels had been scratched away. The youngest boy clutched a cup to his mouth and licked the last drops from it.

Jo lowered her lamp. “We’re not patrol.”

The old man stared at Morrow. “Everything with a lens is patrol.”

Nia took out her canteen. There was less than a mouthful left. She poured it into the boy’s cup.

Jo inhaled sharply but said nothing.

The woman’s eyes fixed on Nia’s hand. “The city told us the tunnels were flooded.”

“The city wanted you to think that,” Nia said.

“No,” Jo murmured. “The city wanted everyone to think there was nowhere else to go.”

The family moved on before them, feeling along the wall toward the southern branch. More people appeared in the dark: two mechanics carrying a filter cartridge between them, a man with a child asleep inside a laundry sack, three women pushing a handcart whose wheels had been wrapped in cloth. They spoke in whispers about patrols and credits, about neighborhoods where taps had become warm and brown, about a district abandoned after the ground cracked beneath its apartments.

At a lower chamber, the tunnel opened over a black pool.

The water reflected their lamps without reflecting their faces. An oily skin shifted across its surface. Morrow dipped a sensor prong and recoiled with a frantic burst of chirps.

Nia read the result on her tablet. Arsenic. Solvents. Lithium salts.

“From the northern mines,” she said.

Jo looked toward the families waiting at the edge. “They know.”

“They may not know what it is.”

“They know it makes children sick.”

A pipe emerged from the ceiling and poured a slow thread into the pool. The pipe was new composite, bright against the old brick. It ran east, toward the reservoir’s buried heart. Nia photographed the joint, the maintenance stamp, the direction arrow. Her mind assembled a chain: runoff into watershed, water diverted from the city, private reserves filled while Cinder Row went dry.

Jo pulled the tablet down. “Not now.”

“When?”

“When we’re not standing beside poison.”

They crossed on a narrow maintenance ledge. On the other side, the tunnel climbed. Air moved through it, carrying the dry smell of dust and dead grass.

Near dawn, they emerged behind a concrete spillway beyond the reservoir fence. Saint Orra lay behind them, its towers pale under the first light. The reservoir itself had shrunk to a gray basin crossed by old channels. Nothing moved on its surface except gulls.

Nia expected relief. Instead she felt the city tugging at every bone.

A line of smoke rose from the direction of Cinder Row.

Jo saw it too. “We keep walking.”

The agricultural belt began where the city’s pavement broke apart. Fields stretched in brittle squares, their irrigation ditches white with mineral crust. Far ahead, a wind pump turned once, shuddered, and stopped.

They made it less than a kilometer before a voice called, “Put the drone down.”

A man stood beside a dead orchard with a rifle held loosely across his chest. He was broad-shouldered, gray at the temples, and wore a scarf over his mouth. Behind him, the soil had gone the color of rust. A child’s swing hung from a bare tree, its seat powdered orange.

Jo stepped between him and Nia. “We’re carrying no weapons.”

“I didn’t ask about weapons.” The man nodded at Morrow. “I asked about the machine.”

“It’s damaged,” Nia said.

“So is my well. We all have something in common.”

He introduced himself as Farid Anwar. He led them to a low farm building where the walls were patched with sheet metal and old election signs. Inside, the air smelled of boiled grain and vinegar. A woman in a red headscarf brought water—not clear, but filtered twice—and set it before them without asking questions.

Nia drank too quickly. Her stomach cramped.

Farid watched the tablet on her knee. “You’re the girl from the wall.”

Nia stiffened. “You saw the broadcast?”

“Everyone saw it who had a wall and a projector. The question is whether everyone saw what came after.”

“Meridian arrested my mother.”

“And your brother?”

“Still in the city.”

Farid’s gaze softened, but only for a moment. “Then you should understand why a picture of a pipeline is not enough.”

“It proves the diversion.”

“It proves one pipe. My fields prove what the water did after the mine began bleeding into the watershed. The refugees camped by the dry canal prove what happens when a harvest fails. The women walking all night for containers prove the rest.” He tapped the tablet. “You have evidence. You do not yet have a movement.”

The woman with the red scarf gave a short laugh. “Farid, don’t frighten them before breakfast.”

“I’m not frightening them. I’m saving us time.”

He took them past the farm to a buried cistern beneath a stand of thorn trees. A radio mast rose from its center, assembled from irrigation pipe and bicycle spokes. Voices murmured from its speaker: a courier reporting a patrol, an engineer requesting a seal, someone in a city clinic listing needed medicines.

“The Open Current,” Farid said. “Not an organization, exactly. A promise that water, information, and people can move without Meridian’s permission.”

Nia listened to the overlapping voices. Routes. Quantities. Names. Needs. A system waiting to be made legible.

“Who coordinates it?” she asked.

“No one does.”

“That’s inefficient.”

“It is difficult,” Farid replied. “Those are not the same thing.”

Nia opened her evidence files. “If you give me access to your stations, I can organize the data, identify the highest-priority failures, and prepare a release that Meridian cannot answer.”

Farid’s expression closed. “There it is.”

“What?”

“The city’s answer to everything. Find the cleverest person, hand her the controls, and call obedience cooperation.”

Jo glanced at Nia. Not accusing. Worse: recognizing.

Nia felt the old certainty rise—the same certainty that had made pipes connect, records align, walls light up. “People are dying because no one is making decisions.”

“People are dying because decisions were made without them,” Farid said. “You may be right about the water. You are not entitled to become another Meridian.”

The radio crackled. A young voice announced that two Saint Orra couriers had reached the southern belt with proof of arrests and a damaged drone.

Everyone in the cistern turned toward Nia.

Morrow chirped once, as if objecting to being called proof.

Nia closed her hand around the wafer beneath her shirt. She had escaped the city, but not the question Jo had carried beside her through the dark: what good was truth if only one person could hold it?

Farid pointed to the radio console. “Sit. Listen first.”

For once, Nia did.

chapters.name: Open Current
chapters.content:
## Open Current

For three hours, Nia listened.

The radio voices arrived in fragments, carried through static and the dry hiss of the agricultural belt. A clinic near the eastern rail line needed distilled water for infants. A farm cooperative had found dead fish in an irrigation ditch. A courier was hiding beneath a grain elevator while Meridian patrols searched the road. Someone in a refugee camp asked whether the promised tankers were real.

No one waited for a central answer. They reported, argued, offered what they could, and moved on.

Nia kept reaching for her tablet.

By the fourth time, Jo closed her fingers around the stylus. “Listen with your whole body.”

“I am listening.”

“You’re calculating.”

“Those aren’t opposites.”

“They are when the calculation makes everyone else into noise.”

Across the cistern room, Farid pretended not to hear. The radio mast above them shivered in the wind, its bicycle spokes clicking like small metal teeth.

A woman came through the doorway carrying a crate of circuit boards. She was tall, dark-skinned, and wore a faded blue medical mask beneath her chin. Her boots were caked with pale soil.

“Dr. Sera Okafor,” Farid said. “Sera, these are the wall girl and the courier.”

“Nia Vale,” Nia corrected.

Sera set down the crate. “The wall girl has a name. Good. Does the name come with a water sample?”

Nia showed her the photograph of the poisoned pool beneath the reservoir and Morrow’s sensor readings. Sera studied them without praise or alarm.

“Your readings are plausible,” she said.

“Plausible?”

“Not proven. Your drone’s sensor partition is damaged. The readings need independent confirmation.”

“They match the mine’s discharge profile.”

“They match a discharge profile.” Sera tapped the screen. “You’re leaping from what the instrument says to what the world must mean.”

A crackling voice interrupted. “Sera, if the north canal is poisoned, do we abandon the settlement?”

Sera leaned toward the microphone. “No. Test the intake, isolate the branch, and send me the numbers.”

“The test kit is missing.”

“Then borrow one.”

“From whom?”

“Ask the people who have one.”

The voice fell silent. Sera turned back. “Evidence is not a speech. It is a practice. You make it, question it, and make it again.”

A young man ducked beneath the doorway carrying a coil of cable and a municipal tool case. He stopped when he saw Nia.

“Nia?”

She knew the voice before the face. The last time she had seen Tomas Vale, he had worn a Meridian badge and told Amara that municipal service required compromises. Nia had been twelve. Tavi had been asleep nearby, wheezing into his pillow. She had called Tomas a traitor. He had left without defending himself.

“Uncle Tomas.”

Jo’s hand moved toward the pocket where she kept the wafer.

Tomas glanced at it. “I’m not here for your records.”

“You worked for Meridian.”

“I worked for the city before Meridian bought the city. I designed maintenance protocols. I resigned when they made the emergency exceptions permanent.”

Nia remembered Amara refusing to speak his name at dinner. She had assumed silence was proof.

Farid picked up the tool case. “Tomas is why the western pump still runs.”

“And why the eastern canal is a ditch,” a farmer called from outside.

A broad woman named Marisol entered with two younger men. Dust filmed her cheeks. “City engineers come here when they need a photograph of suffering,” she said. “Then they leave with our measurements and send us a plan that kills the orchard.”

“We have not sent you a plan,” Tomas said.

“You’re about to.”

The room filled: farm workers, radio operators, three refugees from the southern camps, and a boy no older than fourteen with a bandage around his forearm. They formed a loose circle around the cistern’s central table. No one took a chair because there were not enough, and no one seemed willing to grant the table authority by standing behind it.

Lio Chen came last, climbing down from the mast platform. She was small and sharp-faced, with two radios strapped across her chest and a green scarf wound around her shaved head. She had spent six years moving between refugee camps and could identify a station by its static.

Lio looked at Morrow. “That machine carries a transmitter.”

“An unstable one,” Nia said.

“Then it’s like the rest of us.”

She connected a cable to the drone’s service port. Morrow chirped and rotated its lens toward Nia.

“Careful. Its memory partition is unstable.”

“So is every memory that lives under occupation.” Lio looked around. “We have one meeting before the tankers decide whether to come. Speak plainly.”

The arguments began.

Marisol demanded that they repair the western canals and save the seed stores before another heat wave. A refugee organizer named Deka said the camps could not wait for harvests that might never return. Tomas proposed sabotaging the coastal pipeline—not destroying it, but forcing pressure into abandoned municipal lines. Sera argued for watershed restoration: dams, reed beds, sealed mine channels, and hundreds of repeated tests.

“Months?” Deka said. “Children cannot drink a future.”

“Then deliver water now,” Sera replied. “But delivery is not a cure.”

Lio lifted one hand. “Exposure?”

Nia had been waiting.

She placed her tablet on the table and projected a map. Blue lines crossed the agricultural belt, converging on three settlement clusters. Red marks showed contamination readings, though she omitted Morrow’s exact sensor logs and the contract fragment naming Helix’s reserve consortium. She told herself the files were too dangerous to expose before they had a secure copy. That was partly true.

The other part was that she wanted the first decisive operation to be hers.

“If we combine pipeline routes, population counts, and current tank capacity,” she said, “we can redirect the next emergency shipment to the maximum number of people. Tomas can interrupt the coastal diversion. Sera’s teams can verify contamination along the reopened branches. Lio can broadcast the results. One coordinated operation gives us immediate relief and proof Meridian cannot dismiss.”

The room quieted.

Nia enlarged the map. “The shipment should come here first, then split north and east. We can serve eleven thousand people in forty-eight hours.”

The bandaged boy leaned closer. “How many at the camps?”

“Approximately six thousand, including temporary arrivals.”

“Your map says four thousand eight hundred.”

Nia looked at him. “That was the last verified count.”

“It changed yesterday.”

“Then update the number.”

“With what?” he asked. “We don’t have your equipment.”

Sera’s eyes flicked toward Nia. Marisol gave a humorless laugh.

There it was: the flaw in the beautiful map. Not that it was wrong, but that everyone outside its boundaries became an error waiting for correction.

A girl named Anik, repairing a radio battery in the corner, pointed at the red marks. “What’s the source?”

“Reservoir sensor records.”

“Whose?”

“Meridian’s, reconstructed by my drone.”

“Then if they call it fabricated?”

“They can’t. The pattern is too consistent.”

“They called my father fabricated,” Deka said.

Nia’s certainty faltered. “People aren’t data.”

“No,” Deka said. “That’s why data has to answer to people.”

Jo had been silent. Now she stepped away from the wall. “Nia, you’re holding back the strongest records.”

Nia felt every face turn toward her.

“I’m protecting them,” she said.

“From Meridian, yes. And from this room.”

“That’s not fair.”

“You decided which pieces everyone was allowed to see. You decided the operation before anyone here agreed there should be one.”

The old anger rose. “Someone has to make a decision.”

Tomas spoke quietly. “That is what I told myself when I signed the first exception.”

Nia stared at him.

“I thought I was buying time,” he continued. “A centralized system could respond faster. A few temporary restrictions would protect the whole city. Then the restrictions became the system, and everyone outside the model became expendable.”

Farid took the tablet and turned off the projection. “The Open Current is not a machine you repair by finding its cleverest part.”

Lio removed one radio and placed it before Nia. “You can have a station. Not control of the network. Send the records you are willing to share, and label what is confirmed, disputed, or missing.”

Sera nodded. “Tomorrow we collect independent samples.”

Marisol said, “Tonight we inspect the western canal.”

Deka added, “And the camps receive half the next tanker, whatever your model says.”

Nia looked from face to face. They were not accepting her plan. They were taking it apart and making something less elegant, slower, and perhaps harder to break.

Morrow gave a soft chirp. Lio touched its casing as if calming an animal.

Nia unlocked the first evidence file. Then, after a long pause, she opened the second.

Jo watched her, not smiling.

It was not trust. It was a door left unlatched.

Outside, the dead orchard clicked in the wind. Inside, voices assigned routes, sample kits, tanker shares, and witnesses. Nia wrote everything down—not as orders, but as questions others could amend.

For the first time since the wall lit up in Cinder Row, her map had no center.

chapters.name: The Wrong Calculation
chapters.content:
## Chapter 6: The Wrong Calculation

The tanker arrived at dawn, its blue sides filmed with dust and its tires sunk halfway into the road.

Every settlement on the western belt had sent someone to watch it come in. They stood along the fence at Farid’s farm with empty cans, folded ration cards, and the strained patience of people who had been promised water too many times. Refugee families from the southern camp clustered beneath a torn shade cloth. Marisol and Tomas argued over a canal map beside the cistern. Lio’s radio clicked from the porch, carrying voices from three other stations.

Nia watched the tanker’s approach on her tablet. The screen showed the model she had built overnight: population density, medical need, distance, evaporation loss, estimated contamination, available storage. Each settlement was a node. Each road was a line. The answer kept returning the same way.

Farid’s farm should receive forty-two percent.

The southern camp, twice as large and with almost no functioning wells, should receive fifty-eight.

But the farm’s seed bank was not a number on the model. Neither was the heat pressing down beneath the pale morning sky. Nia had entered the seed bank as agricultural inventory, a future benefit weighted against immediate human need. The calculation had not hesitated.

She had.

Then she had remembered Tavi’s cough, the vaporizer’s thin mechanical hiss, and the way Meridian had turned his need into a reason to deny the whole family water. She had told herself that a system that saved the most lives was better than a system that protected whoever shouted nearest to the tank.

The tanker driver climbed down. “Destination list says Anwar settlement first.”

“That’s the old list,” Nia said.

Farid turned from the cistern. “Old?”

Nia felt every face shift toward her. “The camp has fewer than six hours of potable reserve. You have storage for two days.”

“Not if the heat holds.”

“It won’t kill anyone today.”

Farid’s expression tightened. “The seeds will.”

Behind him, the shade cloth lifted in a hot gust. Beyond it lay the seed shed, a low structure patched with tin and mud plaster. Inside were jars of millet, beans, salt grass, and the black drought corn Farid’s grandmother had carried across two borders. Sera had explained that the collection represented decades of adaptation. Losing it would not merely mean losing this season.

Nia knew that. She had put the value into the model. She had simply decided the model’s answer mattered more.

“People cannot drink heritage,” she said, too quickly.

Farid stared at her as if she had struck him. “No. But people cannot eat your percentage either.”

Jo stepped between them. “Nia, what did you change?”

“The allocation route.”

“Without the council?”

“There wasn’t time.” Nia turned to the driver. “Take the tanker to the southern camp. Distribute the farm’s share there, then return with the second vehicle if—”

“If?” Farid repeated.

The tanker engine coughed to life.

For one second Nia believed the movement of the machine would settle the argument. Decisions always looked cleaner once they were in motion. The road would carry the water where it was most needed. The figures would become people, and the people would survive.

Farid seized the driver’s door.

Tomas caught his arm. “Not here.”

“Move,” Farid said.

The driver looked from one man to the other, then at Nia. “Who signs?”

Nia reached for the tablet. “I do.”

Jo’s hand closed around her wrist. “You don’t.”

The tanker rolled away before either of them could stop it, leaving a low brown cloud over the road.

By noon, the temperature had climbed past the warning line painted on Farid’s thermometer. The cistern’s level dropped as families filled bottles for the camp. Farid and Marisol carried the last buckets toward the seed shed, setting them beneath the roof where they could be poured over the cooling pipes. Nia followed with a wrench, though no tool could repair the decision she had made.

Inside, the air smelled of dust and old grain. Farid opened the first jar. The seeds were dull and small, each one holding a season that had not yet happened.

“We need to keep the humidity stable,” he said. “The cooling unit has twelve hours.”

“Can we run it from the pump battery?”

“Not and keep the cistern filter alive.”

Nia looked at the jars. “Then we prioritize the most viable varieties.”

Farid laughed once, without humor. “You heard yourself?”

“I’m trying to help.”

“You are trying to optimize the wreckage.”

Outside, a child began crying. The sound traveled through the thin walls. Nia’s throat constricted. She wanted to say that the camp contained hundreds of children, that three clinics had reported dehydration, that the larger number had not been invented. But Farid was not disputing the camp’s need.

He was disputing her right to decide whose need counted first.

The cooling unit clicked off.

By evening, the jars had begun to sweat. By midnight, the first black corn split in its cloth pouch. The next morning, the western field lay silvered with dead leaves. The young millet had curled into itself. Bean blossoms fell when touched. Farid walked between the rows without speaking, his boots crushing the brittle soil.

The Open Current gathered in the machine shed because there was nowhere else large enough. Voices crowded the heat.

“You diverted a shipment assigned by three stations,” Marisol said. “You altered the route code and forged a confirmation from Lio’s relay.”

“I did not forge it. I used the emergency authorization protocol.”

“Which no one authorized you to use,” Lio said over the radio speaker. Her voice came thinly from the coast road. “You found a loophole and called it consent.”

Nia held up her tablet. “The camp’s reserve was lower. Their population is larger. The allocation prevented more immediate deaths.”

“And destroyed the seed bank,” Sera said. “Did your model know the bank contained varieties resistant to the northern solvent?”

Nia hesitated.

Sera’s eyes hardened. “Of course it didn’t. It knew what you gave it.”

Farid entered last. Dust coated his trousers. He carried a cracked jar in both hands.

“This is the black corn,” he said. “It survived three failed rains and the mine dust. My mother saved it from a government warehouse fire. I was supposed to plant it next month.” He set the jar on the table. “You sent water away from this place because your map showed a larger population elsewhere. You treated us as variables, Nia. Variables can be moved without asking.”

“I was trying to save people.”

“I know.” His voice was quieter than anger. “That is what makes it dangerous.”

The room divided before anyone announced that it had. Marisol demanded Nia be removed from all allocation work. Two young couriers defended her, saying the camp’s children would have died without the shipment. Tomas said both things could be true. Jo remained beside the door, pale and silent, until Nia looked at her.

“Say it,” Nia said.

Jo swallowed. “You made Meridian’s argument in a different voice.”

The words landed harder than Farid’s accusation. Nia remembered the city screens: neutral algorithms, unavoidable priorities, unfortunate losses. She had hated them because they concealed a choice. Now she could see her own choice shining through every clean line on the tablet.

Sera broke the silence. “There is another problem.”

She placed a data wafer on the table. Its casing had been burned along one edge. “The complete routing archive is gone. Morrow’s copy ends before the contract authorization. The purge reached the pump array’s redundant storage.”

Nia stared at the wafer. “You recovered this?”

“Fragments. Enough to show transfers. Not enough to prove who ordered them.”

“The sensor logs—”

“Show contamination readings, but not an unbroken chain of custody. Meridian will call them altered. Helix will call them mine noise. Without the authorization page and the original timestamps, your conspiracy is an interpretation.”

Nia’s hand found Morrow beneath the table. The drone’s casing was warm from the afternoon, its damaged transmitter ticking softly.

An interpretation. The phrase opened a hollow space inside her. She had believed the records were a door: obtain them, show them, and the truth would force the city to change. Now half the door had burned away. What remained could be dismissed, just as easily as the families who had trusted her could be dismissed as acceptable losses.

Farid lifted the cracked jar. “You can stay,” he said. “But you do not choose for this settlement again. Not without a meeting. Not without the people carrying the consequences.”

Marisol pointed toward the road. “Others think she should leave before the network becomes her machine.”

“And others think expelling her wastes the one person who understands the infrastructure,” Tomas said.

Nia expected Jo to decide for them. Instead Jo looked at the jar, then at Nia.

“Make the choice yourself,” she said. “For once, without calculating what the rest of us are worth.”

Nia opened the allocation file. The values waited in obedient rows. She could change the weights, add a variable for seed memory, create a better model. The old instinct rose immediately: fix the equation, prove the failure was technical, make herself useful enough that no one could remove her.

She closed the file.

“I don’t know how to repair this,” she said.

The admission did not restore the crops. It did not bring back the missing records or fill the empty cistern. No one forgave her. But the room grew still, and in that stillness Nia understood the first fact her calculations had excluded.

Being right was not the same as being trusted.

And a solution imposed on people could become another kind of theft.
