chapters.name: Many Witnesses
chapters.content:
## Many Witnesses

Sera put the first sample bottle on the table between them as if it were evidence in a trial.

It was no larger than Nia’s thumb, stoppered with wax and marked in blue pencil: WESTERN DITCH, DAWN, 06:10. A gray skin floated on the water inside. When Sera tilted it, the skin broke into shining fragments that clung to the glass.

“Your archive says the runoff entered the northern watershed three weeks before the first fish died,” Sera said. “It might be right. Morrow’s sensors might be right. But if we carry that conclusion to every settlement and ask them to risk their lives on it, we need more than might.”

Nia folded her arms. “We have the mine coordinates, the chemical signatures, and a pipeline that disappears under the Authority’s maps.”

“We have fragments.” Sera tapped the bottle. “Fragments are not a chain.”

Behind them, the cistern yard stirred awake. Farid’s surviving goats complained from their pen. Tomas rolled a coil of cable across the packed earth, and Lio’s radio clicked through a list of camps waiting for water. The seed bank’s ruined cooling shed stood open to the white morning. Inside, cracked jars rested in rows like small, broken teeth.

Nia looked away from them.

“We can publish the fragments with a warning,” she said. “Confirmed, probable, disputed, missing. I can build a confidence model.”

“Another model,” Jo said.

She had been leaning against the cistern wall, her orange satchel at her feet. Dust had gathered at the edges of her boots. She looked tired enough to sleep standing, but her eyes were fixed on Nia.

Nia’s throat tightened. “A model would tell people what we know.”

“A model would tell people what you decide they know.”

The words landed harder than Sera’s challenge. Nia opened her mouth, then closed it. In the tablet’s dark screen she saw her own reflection: hollow cheeks, hair tied with wire, an expression that had become permanently defensive.

Sera lifted the bottle. “We begin again. Not by throwing away Morrow. By making it one witness among many.”

They spent the day turning the farm into a workshop. Tomas found old housings in a municipal crate, each stamped with a Meridian inventory number. Lio stripped copper from a dead radio and showed two refugee teenagers how to solder leads without burning through the insulation. Sera explained that a sensor station did not need to be clever. It needed to be visible, replaceable, and difficult for one person to falsify.

At Farid’s request, the first station went beside the western ditch, where the soil was still pale from the dead crop. Its casing was a blue cooking pot with holes drilled through the lid. A temperature probe hung below the waterline. Another measured conductivity. A paper card, sealed in waxed cloth, listed the date, time, weather, and name of every person who touched it.

“Why names?” one of the teenagers asked.

“So nobody becomes an invisible authority,” Sera said. “And so nobody carries blame alone when a thing breaks.”

Nia installed the transmitter. Her fingers knew the work more quickly than her mind did: strip, twist, solder, seal. When she finished, the station blinked once and sent a burst toward the radio mast.

The tablet filled with numbers.

She reached to lock the feed.

Jo caught her wrist.

“Don’t.”

“It needs a filter. Raw readings invite sabotage.”

“Raw readings invite questions.”

“They invite people to mistake noise for truth.”

Jo did not let go. “That’s what Meridian said. The public couldn’t understand the system. The public would panic. The public needed a clean answer.”

Nia pulled free. “I am not Meridian.”

“No. You’re more frightening.”

A silence opened around them. Even the soldering stopped.

Jo’s face changed, regret crossing it too late to soften the blow. “You believe you’re different because you’re right,” she said. “But you took a shipment, hid the route, and made everyone else live inside your calculation. Meridian did the same thing with better equipment.”

Nia stared at the blinking station. The temptation was immediate and physical: take the transmitter, rewrite the permissions, keep the system safe. She could prevent false readings. She could identify malicious inputs. She could make a single clean map out of the mess.

She could make the mess disappear.

Farid arrived carrying a shovel across one shoulder. “If you’re finished arguing over my ditch,” he said, “I have a condition.”

Nia turned. “What condition?”

“You want my land to prove the mines poisoned it. Fine. But this project does not exist only to make Helix look guilty.” He pointed toward the dead western field. “You measure the water, then you help us bring it back. Samples, drainage, soil beds, whatever Sera says. If the readings show a way to save the ditch, that matters as much as the story.”

Nia almost answered with a calculation. The population served by the field was smaller than the southern camp. The labor might produce less immediate water. The political value of a documented contamination event could be enormous.

She stopped before the words formed.

“What do you need first?” she asked.

Farid studied her as though the question itself might be a trick. “The east sluice is clogged with mining silt. Clear it before the next storm. If there is a next storm.”

Nia looked at Tomas. “Can we clear it without sending the sludge downstream?”

“Not without a settling trench.”

“Then we dig one.”

Farid nodded once. It was not forgiveness, but it was an opening.

By evening, three more stations had been assigned. One would travel with Lio to the refugee camps, where families could test tanker water before accepting it. One would be installed in a Cinder Row apartment block by a courier who knew the illegal pipe network. The third would remain at the farm, watched in shifts by Farid’s neighbors.

Nia designed the station ledger. Every reading would carry its raw value, its instrument condition, its weather, and the names of witnesses. Anyone could attach a correction or dispute, but no correction could erase the original. A disagreement would become another layer on the map.

At first she made the access rules so strict that even Sera needed Nia’s approval to add a station. Lio read the draft aloud over the radio and laughed without humor.

“Congratulations,” she said. “You have invented a smaller Meridian.”

Nia deleted the approval requirement.

Then the dispute function failed.

A camp station reported arsenic at a level that would make the water dangerous. Nia compared it with Morrow’s old readings and marked the result probable contamination. The next morning, a camp nurse named Binta sent a correction: the sensor had been stored beside a battery acid spill. The reading was false, but the mistake had delayed distribution while families argued over whether the tanker was safe.

Nia felt vindicated and ashamed at the same time.

“See?” she told Jo. “This is why uncontrolled data is dangerous.”

Jo was crouched beside the station, replacing its corroded contact. “No. This is why data needs people who can say where it came from.”

“And if the people lie?”

“Then other people answer them.”

The answer was infuriating because it did not solve anything. It offered no guarantee, no perfect threshold, no protective wall between truth and error. Only a process that could be watched.

That night, Nia sat with the families whose water she had redirected. A mother from the southern camp described the relief of receiving the tanker and the fear of hearing that Farid’s seeds had died for it. An old farmer named Deka told Nia he would rather accept less water regularly than depend on a heroic delivery that vanished without warning. A child asked whether the blue station could tell them when the next tanker would come.

“No,” Nia said. “It can tell us what has happened. The decision about what comes next belongs to the people affected.”

The child frowned. “Then what good is it?”

Nia looked at the paper cards drying on the table, each covered with names in different hands. “It gives us something to decide from together.”

Before dawn, she and Farid went to the east sluice. The mud sucked at their boots. They worked without speaking until the shovel struck a buried length of composite pipe, black and smooth beneath the silt.

Farid’s hand tightened on the handle. “Another one.”

Nia knelt beside it. Morrow’s camera could record the pipe, but the image alone would be called fabrication. She took out the notebook instead.

“Who saw this first?” she asked.

Farid looked toward the ridge, where two neighbors were approaching with tools. “All of us, soon enough.”

He called them over. Sera came with a sample kit. Tomas brought a measuring rod. Lio arrived carrying the radio, breathless from the climb. Even Jo, who had been checking the camp relay, appeared at the ditch’s edge.

Nia wrote the date. She recorded the weather, the pipe’s depth, the direction of its slope. Then she handed the notebook to Farid.

“Add what I missed.”

He took it. His first mark corrected her estimate of the ditch’s position by nearly a meter.

Nia let him keep the page.

By sunrise, the station beside the ditch had a new entry: five witnesses, one disputed pipe, a sample awaiting testing, and a plan to build a settling trench before the water moved again. The truth was no longer a thing Nia carried out of the dark. It had become heavier, slower, and harder to control.

For the first time, she thought that might be why it could survive.

chapters.name: The Living Map
chapters.content:
## Chapter 8: The Living Map

By dawn, the east sluice had become a wound with people working around it.

The buried composite pipe lay on trestles beside the ditch, its cut end wrapped in clear sheeting. Sera had marked three sample bottles with times, names, and the direction of the wind. Farid stood knee-deep in mud, directing Tomas toward a bank of reeds that had survived the last dry season.

“Not there,” Farid called. “The roots hold the bank. Cut behind them.”

Tomas lowered his shovel. “The old survey says the bank is stable.”

“The old survey did not watch it flood.”

Tomas looked at Nia. Once, she would have chosen between them by comparing the survey to the soil gradient. Now she crouched and pressed two fingers into the mud. It trembled with water beneath the crust.

“Farid’s right,” she said. “The survey’s from before the diversion.”

Farid gave her a brief glance, not approval exactly, but acknowledgment. It warmed her more than approval would have.

They dug the settling trench in three shallow turns instead of one deep channel. Tomas calculated the slope. Farid chose the reeds and the placement of woven root mats. Refugees from the southern camp hauled stones in baskets, while two children carried handfuls of the cleanest gravel and argued over whose pile was straighter. The trench would not cleanse the watershed. Sera had repeated that until everyone could say it with her. It would slow contaminated silt long enough for them to test, separate, and decide what could be planted.

A week earlier, Nia would have opened her tablet and produced the best design. Today she held the tablet under her arm and listened.

At midday, a runner arrived from the western canal with news that the gate had jammed. Tomas gathered his tools. Nia followed, expecting a mechanical failure. The gate was not jammed. A fig tree’s roots had lifted the stone channel and turned the water toward a field that the old maps labeled abandoned.

“It is not abandoned,” said Marisol, the farmer who owned the field. “It is resting.”

The distinction mattered. The network’s first canal map showed a dead branch in gray. Marisol drew a line through the gray with a grease pencil.

“During the next heat,” she said, “this branch carries water to the refugee kitchens. The old channel is cracked, but the route is still here.”

Nia photographed the correction. Then she entered it into the platform she had begun building at night.

She called it Current Map, though Jo said the name sounded like something sold in a municipal office.

“It is a living map,” Nia said.

“It is a collection of arguments wearing coordinates.”

“That is less memorable.”

“More honest.”

So Nia made the arguments visible.

Every allocation appeared as a colored path: blue for water released, amber for water promised but not yet delivered, white for a request under discussion. Beside each path were the names of the assembly that had approved it, the number of households affected, the evidence used, and a place for objections. No entry could be erased. A correction became a second line beneath the first, and a reversal remained attached to both.

The old version of Nia would have called that inefficient. The new version watched a camp mechanic challenge her estimate of storage loss and change the numbers.

“You assumed the tanks are full at dawn,” he said over the radio. “They are not. We drain them at night to stop the heat from growing algae.”

“Why wasn’t that in the station report?”

“Because the station reports pressure, not habits.”

Nia stared at the figures. His correction shifted the southern camp’s request by nine hundred liters. Her first impulse was to defend the model. Her second was to ask him to demonstrate the measurement. Her third, quieter now, was gratitude.

“Add it as a local condition,” she said. “Name yourself.”

“I don’t need my name.”

“The record does.”

“Then name the kitchen crew. We all drain them.”

She did.

At Farid’s farm, the first allocation assembly met beneath a shade cloth patched with flour sacks. Representatives came from three farms, the refugee camp, two traveling settlements, and a Cinder Row contact speaking through Jo’s radio. Saint Orra’s neighborhoods were not physically present, but their voices arrived in bursts of static: families with no cisterns, families still connected to the illegal blue-tubing lines, families who could contribute labor but not water.

The question was how to divide the next tanker.

Nia projected the map onto a sheet. The routes crossed one another like veins. She showed the shortage, the estimated arrival times, and the cost of sending water north before the heat peaked.

A woman from the camp raised her hand. “Your map makes our kitchens a single point. We are not one point.”

Nia paused. “What should it show?”

“Seven kitchens. Two have children with fever. One has a broken pump. If you combine us, the broken pump disappears.”

Nia split the symbol into seven.

A Cinder Row voice crackled through Jo’s receiver. “And don’t mark us as recipients only. We can send filters and repair parts through the courier route.”

Jo smiled without looking at Nia. “Put that on the map.”

Nia did. The lines changed again. Water moved one way; labor, filters, seed cuttings, and information moved another. The map stopped looking like a pipeline and began to resemble a conversation.

Morrow watched from the table, its bottle-glass lens dusty, three rotors tucked close to its body. When Nia powered it on, the drone gave a weak chirp. The children crowded near.

“Does it belong to Nia?” one asked.

Nia looked at the machine. For months she had hidden it under her coat, slept with one hand on its case, and treated every file inside it as something only she could interpret. Now Lio had fitted a new transmitter from two broken radios. Tomas had rebuilt its landing brace. Sera had labeled its old sensor readings beside the community samples. Farid had made a weatherproof perch from a seed crate.

“No,” Nia said. “It belongs to the work.”

The child frowned. “Can I fly it?”

“Not alone.”

“Can I learn?”

“Yes.”

Morrow rose unevenly, wobbling into the pale air. Lio guided its signal from one radio station to the next. The drone’s camera sent back the wetland basin: a shallow crescent of water, reed beds planted by camp volunteers, and black silt held behind the new stone check. Not restored, not safe, but alive.

The image traveled across the mesh to Saint Orra and the farms beyond. People added notes. A woman in Cinder Row identified an old drainage outlet. A boy at the camp spotted a dead patch spreading along the southern reeds. Sera marked it for sampling. Nobody asked Nia whether the image was true. They compared it with what they knew.

That evening, Jo found her beside the cistern, staring at the map’s growing web.

“You gave it away,” Jo said.

“I built permissions.”

“You gave it away.”

Nia considered denying it, then let the denial pass. “It feels like losing a limb.”

“Good. Maybe you’ll stop trying to carry the whole body.”

Nia laughed, though the sound caught. “You could be kinder.”

“I am being kinder. I’m still here.”

Lio interrupted from the radio table. “We have a packet from the north relay. Intercepted, not verified.”

The room quieted.

The packet had been copied from a Helix maintenance channel. Sera read the first lines aloud: wetland sites, phase two, removal before inspection. Another line named three locations, including Farid’s east basin. The final instruction was blunt: ensure attribution to Open Current extremists; use their symbols if available.

Farid’s hand tightened around the edge of the table. “When?”

“Tomorrow night,” Lio said. “Maybe. The timestamp is damaged.”

Nia felt the old answer surge up: strike first, choose the targets, command the response. The map glowed beside her, full of names and disagreements and corrections.

“Mark it as intercepted and unverified,” she said. “No one treats it as fact yet.”

“And if it is true?” Jo asked.

“Then every wetland assembly decides how to guard its site. We share the warning, the source limits, and the evidence needed to confirm it.”

Farid looked toward the dark basin. “That takes longer than sending orders.”

“Yes.” Nia swallowed. “But orders are what they’ll use to say we did it.”

Tomas began listing watch rotations. Sera requested water tests before anyone moved sediment. Lio prepared a broadcast that included the uncertainty instead of hiding it. Jo contacted the camps. On the wall, Nia added a new color: violet, for danger under investigation.

The living map changed once more—not into certainty, but readiness. It showed what they knew, what they did not, and who would decide what happened next.

Outside, the wetland held the last light in its shallow water. Beneath the reeds, something small moved, and the surface closed over it without a sound.

chapters.content:
## Chapter 9: The Price of Proof

The first thing Meridian took was the light.

At dusk, every lamp in Cinder Row went dark at once. The apartment blocks became black teeth against the reservoir haze. Pumps stopped. Radios hissed and died. Somewhere below Nia’s window, a child began to cry, and the cry traveled through the stairwell as if the building itself had found a voice.

Jo held a hand-crank receiver between them. “They cut the rebellious districts.”

“Not the whole grid,” Nia said, watching Aurelia Heights shine across the water. “Only the districts listed as noncompliant.”

On the Current Map, the city’s outage reports appeared one by one through the mesh: Cinder Row, South Foundry, the western refugee camps. The coastal enclaves remained bright. Their private reservoirs still had power.

Then Meridian’s broadcast broke through on a battery radio.

“Citizens of Saint Orra,” said a calm official voice, “the organization styling itself the Open Current has attacked public infrastructure, endangered water security, and threatened lawful workers. Its members are terrorists. Emergency restrictions will continue until order is restored.”

A photograph followed: Farid’s east basin, the reed beds black against the sky. The image had been altered to show fire where there had been none. Beneath it, a red symbol resembling the Current Map’s violet warning mark pulsed beside the words EXTREMIST SABOTAGE.

Nia’s stomach turned. “They’re using our records.”

“They’re using our shape,” Jo said. “That’s different.”

At Farid’s farm, the attack began before midnight.

The first charge blew the western settling trench apart. Mud and chemical-smelling water rolled through the reeds. The second destroyed a sensor mast. Sera and Tomas reached the basin with buckets and sandbags, but the men who had planted the charges were already gone. Morrow’s camera caught only three blurred figures moving beyond the fence, their coats marked with the silver thread used by Helix contractors.

Farid stood in the wash, one boot submerged in black water. “They want the basin poisoned before inspectors arrive.”

Sera knelt beside a broken station. “We need to preserve the fragments. Don’t touch the casing.”

“People are drinking from the upstream cistern.”

“Then Tomas, take the north valve. Lio, broadcast a hold on basin water. Nia, log every action and every uncertainty.”

Nia opened the Current Map with shaking hands. The old impulse came hard: close the permissions, seize the channels, tell everyone where to go. Instead she entered the damage as witnessed, marked Morrow’s footage as partial, and asked the nearest assembly to confirm the evacuation route.

Farid looked at her. “You’re writing while my field dies.”

“I know.”

“No. You know how to write that it died.”

The accusation struck deeper because it was true. For months she had believed proof could stand between people and violence, as if a complete enough record would force the world to become reasonable. Now the evidence lay in mud, and men with guns had walked away from it.

At dawn, a convoy arrived from the east road. No uniforms. No insignia. Three black utility trucks and a municipal surveyor carrying a contract in a waterproof sleeve.

“Helix Meridian offers a private remediation agreement,” the surveyor announced. “Mr. Anwar will sell the basin and the adjoining fields. In return, his family receives relocation credits and protection.”

Farid laughed once. It had no humor in it. “Protection from the men you brought?”

The surveyor’s face tightened. “Refusal will be interpreted as cooperation with a terrorist organization.”

Farid took the contract, folded it, and fed it into the cook fire.

Nia saw the silver-threaded coats at the edge of the field. One of the men lifted a hand. A shot cracked across the morning.

Farid staggered. Jo caught his shoulder, but the second shot dropped him into the mud beside the ruined trench. The trucks turned before anyone could reach them. Their tires threw a fan of brown water over the reeds.

For a moment, no one moved.

Then Nia was on her knees. Farid’s blood spread through his shirt, bright and impossible. Sera pressed both hands to the wound. Tomas shouted for the emergency kit. Lio called every relay at once, her voice breaking through static.

Farid’s eyes found Nia. “Don’t make me a symbol,” he whispered.

She bent close. “You’re going to live.”

“Don’t make me a symbol,” he said again. “Make them remember the field.”

He died before the medics from the southern camp arrived.

They buried him beside the orchard, where the soil was still safe enough for the few surviving trees. Nobody made a speech. The radio carried only his name, the time of his death, the witnesses, and the fact of his refusal. Nia stood with mud dried on her knees and understood that truth was not a shield. It was a responsibility people could be killed for carrying.

That afternoon, another message reached the farm. Amara Vale had been transferred from Saint Orra Detention Center to Facility 12, three hundred kilometers north, beyond the ordinary prisoner routes. No charge was listed. No visitation request would be accepted.

Nia read the notice twice. “They’re moving her because they know we’re trying to reach her.”

“Or because they’re moving everyone,” Sera said gently. “We can’t claim the reason without evidence.”

Nia looked at the blank line where the transfer authorization should have been. “I hate that you’re right.”

“Good. Hate is not proof either.”

Jo’s radio clicked. She turned away to answer, then turned back with a face gone pale. “Tavi’s worse.”

The contact in Cinder Row had reached him through the blue-tubing network. His inhaler was nearly empty. The apartment vaporizer had failed during the blackout, and the family’s distilled water had been seized in the morning search. He was coughing too hard to sleep.

Nia pressed her fist against her mouth. The whole network seemed to narrow to one small room: Tavi curled beneath a blanket, Amara gone, clean water measured in spoonfuls.

“We need an extraction,” she said. “Now.”

“We need a route, a driver, and a clinic willing to take him,” Jo replied. “Not an order.”

Around the map table, grief became argument. Some members demanded a central emergency command. With Farid dead, they said, hesitation was a luxury. Nia had the strongest technical knowledge, the widest records, and the fastest model. Give her the channels, the routes, the guard rotations. Let one person decide until the crisis passed.

“Meridian wins if we debate while people are dying,” said a camp organizer.

“Meridian wins if we become unable to act without one voice,” Jo answered.

The organizer pointed at Nia. “She can save time.”

Nia felt the terrible seduction of it. She could see the map whole: every cistern, road, clinic, relay, and threatened wetland. If everyone obeyed one schedule, they might reach Tavi. They might protect the remaining sites. They might find the men who killed Farid.

“Give me the command key,” she said.

Silence followed. Jo’s face closed, not in surprise but disappointment.

Sera placed a blood-stained sample bag on the table. “And when they capture you?”

“I won’t be captured.”

“Farid said that the morning he died?”

Nia flinched.

Sera continued, quietly. “A system that depends on one person’s certainty is not resilient. It is a single point of failure. You know this technically.”

Jo stepped nearer. “You told us the map belonged to the work. Not to you. If you take every channel now, you turn yourself into Meridian with better intentions.”

The words hurt because they did not feel like an insult. They felt like a hand held out over a drop.

Nia looked at Farid’s empty chair. “Then we need speed without obedience.”

She divided the emergency functions among local assemblies: the Cinder Row couriers would move distilled water and inhaler parts; two camp mechanics would confirm the route; Jo would coordinate the clinic contact; Lio would keep the radio traffic distributed; Tomas would organize wetland watches; Sera would preserve the sabotage evidence. Every decision would carry a named witness and an expiration time.

No one received the command key.

By nightfall, Tavi’s contact reported that the water had reached the apartment. Not enough to cure him. Enough to run the vaporizer for one hour.

Nia listened to his thin, ragged breathing through the radio. “I’m coming,” she said.

His voice was barely audible. “Bring Mom.”

“I will.”

It was a promise she could not yet keep. She made it anyway, then entered it into the map—not as proof, not as a plan, but as an obligation shared with everyone who heard her say it.

Beyond the farm, the ruined wetland shone under a powerless sky. Farid’s orchard stood dark around his grave. The network kept moving, slower than a command and stronger than a command, carrying water, warnings, names, and grief from one frightened hand to another.

## The Mesh

By dawn, the farm had become a collection of listening points.

A radio leaned against the cracked cistern. Another hung from the orchard fence, its wire antenna trembling whenever the wind crossed the dead branches. Someone had carried a receiver to the refugee road and wired it to a bicycle dynamo. At the east wetland, where Farid’s settling trench lay broken and black, Sera’s sensor blinked in three colors: green for power, amber for a disputed reading, red for poison.

The stations did not agree yet. That was the point.

Nia sat beneath the shade cloth with Morrow opened across her knees. The drone’s bottle-glass lens reflected the pale sky. Its transmitter was a scar of solder and salvaged copper, and every time she touched the contact pins, a small blue spark leapt like a nervous insect.

“It still thinks it has a wing,” Jo said.

Morrow gave a thin mechanical chirp.

“It has one and a half wings,” Nia said. “That is different.”

“Tell it that when it falls on your head.”

Across from them, Lio was stripping insulation from a cable with her teeth. She had slept in bursts since the blackout began, moving between the farm, the refugee camps, and the relay points where people waited for news. Her eyes were red, but her hands remained exact.

“The old grid is listening for a single voice,” she said. “So we stop giving it one.”

Nia looked at the map spread on the table. Each station was a colored pin. Farid’s farm. The camps along the dry belt. Cinder Row, where the blue-tubing families were hiding in dark apartments. South Foundry. Three canal crews. A clinic near the northern road. More pins appeared every hour, carried by couriers who arrived with cracked radios and questions written on scraps of packaging.

“How many?” Nia asked.

“Enough to make the signal ugly.”

“Lio.”

“Two hundred and twelve confirmed. More listening than transmitting. If each station passes a packet to two others, and those two pass it onward, Meridian cannot cut the head off the message because there is no head.”

Nia turned the transmitter board over. “Morrow can carry the packets, but not the traffic. The memory partition is damaged. It will have to forget old messages.”

“Then every station keeps a copy,” Lio said. “A message is not safe because one machine remembers it. It is safe because many people can repeat it.”

The sentence entered Nia more deeply than a technical solution should have. For months she had guarded the records as if truth were a fragile instrument, something that could be ruined by an untrained hand. Now Lio was asking hundreds of hands to hold it.

Sera arrived with mud up to her knees and a paper strip sealed in a sample sleeve. “The east basin reading is confirmed by the western ditch,” she said. “Not identical concentrations. Same solvent signature, rising after the discharge window. The camp station has a third reading.”

Nia entered the numbers into the Current Map. “Witness names?”

“Three at the ditch. Two at the camp. One of the camp instruments was exposed to battery acid last week.”

“Flagged as disputed?”

“Flagged, not erased.”

Sera’s gaze held hers. “You’re learning.”

Nia almost smiled. “Slowly.”

They built the mesh through the morning. Tomas brought lengths of municipal cable and showed teenagers how to splice them without sealing the joints against inspection. Refugees mounted stations on cart axles. Farmers tied antennas to irrigation poles. Lio wrote a four-line protocol in grease pencil: identify the sender, mark the time, attach the raw reading, name the uncertainty. No command could enter the network without a place, a person, and an expiration.

When a relay failed, the nearest assembly did not wait for Nia. It rerouted around the dead station. When someone sent an accusation without evidence, three stations asked for a witness and marked the claim unconfirmed. When a repair crew found an old canal gate that could be opened, they transmitted the instructions, the risks, and the amount of water it would release. The map changed under Nia’s fingers, not as a picture of a system but as the system thinking aloud.

At noon, Lio handed Nia the microphone.

“Your account is ready,” she said. “The one with the dates, routes, samples, and missing pages.”

Nia looked toward Farid’s empty chair beside the orchard. She had wanted, once, to make the truth unavoidable by speaking it perfectly. She had imagined the city falling silent before the clean sequence of her proof.

“Broadcast it,” Jo said. “But don’t make it a verdict.”

Nia pressed the switch.

“This is Nia Vale, transmitting through the Open Current mesh. What follows is a documented account, not a complete answer. The records show reservoir water diverted from Saint Orra during emergency cutoffs. Morrow’s surviving logs show routes toward private coastal reserves. Independent stations now record contamination entering the northern watershed. Some evidence is incomplete. Some claims remain disputed. Here are the files. Here are the methods. Here are the names of the people who witnessed the readings.”

She sent the archive in pieces: the pipeline coordinates, the maintenance schedules, the sensor chains, the contract fragment with its missing authorization page. She described what they knew and what they did not know. Then she stopped speaking.

For several seconds, there was only static.

A station in Cinder Row answered first. A woman named Deka read the water schedule taped inside her building’s maintenance cabinet. The cutoff hours matched Nia’s records. A boy from South Foundry transmitted the pressure readings from a public hydrant. The numbers fell whenever Aurelia Heights’ reservoir gates opened. A clinic worker compared the timing with patients turned away from distilled-water treatment.

The proof did not arrive as applause. It arrived as correction.

A coastal worker interrupted from an enclave called Pelagos Nine. His voice shook so badly that Lio had to ask him to repeat himself. He said he worked on the private pipeline Nia had mapped. He gave the pipe diameter, the night-shift schedule, and the names of two pump stations. Another worker contradicted one valve location, then sent a maintenance photograph. A third explained where the line entered the desalination reserve.

“We were told it was emergency infrastructure,” the first worker said. “We were told the city was too unstable to know.”

On the farm, nobody moved.

Then a new packet arrived—not from a sensor, but from inside Meridian.

The sender identified himself only as Technician 6A. Attached was a compressed copy of the Allocation Engine’s source code, signed with a maintenance key and mirrored by four independent stations. The code was dense, full of variables Nia recognized and comments she did not. Sera read over her shoulder. Tomas leaned close. Jo stood behind them, one hand on the back of Nia’s chair.

“There,” Nia said.

A function named CIVIC_STABILITY adjusted priority scores. Another assigned a protection multiplier to districts with “economic continuity value.” The words were not in the public specifications. They were buried beneath neutral language: efficiency, risk, resilience.

“Political priorities,” Sera whispered. “Hard-coded.”

“Not exactly,” Nia said. “They made them look like consequences of the data.”

“Which is worse,” Jo said. “At least a tyrant has to admit he’s choosing.”

The mesh carried the code outward. Technicians began explaining it in ordinary language. A woman in an Aurelia maintenance room described the protected multiplier. A former municipal auditor sent old allocation tables showing how the hidden values had changed before elections. Each account was marked with its source and uncertainty. No one voice could claim to own the revelation.

By evening, Saint Orra had begun to answer.

Families in Cinder Row opened blue-tubing connections through basement walls and ran them toward the apartments where displaced people were sheltering. A mechanic in South Foundry used a stolen pressure gauge to balance the flow. A grandmother sent a warning that one branch was contaminated and should not be opened until Sera’s team tested it. In Aurelia Heights, three households unlocked a service gate and invited water carriers from the dark districts inside.

Meridian’s grid still showed official silence. Its broadcasts continued to call the Open Current a terrorist movement. But beneath that silence, thousands of small stations repeated one another: a reading, a repair, a name, a need, a correction.

Morrow lifted from the table on its remaining rotor and wobbled toward the cistern mast. Nia reached to catch it, then stopped herself.

Lio laughed. “Let it choose its route.”

The drone clipped the mast, recovered, and settled onto a bracket Tomas had built. Its transmitter light turned green. Across the map, new points appeared.

Nia watched them spread—not outward from her, but toward one another. She understood then that the broadcast had not succeeded because she had finally spoken clearly. It had succeeded because people had compared what they knew and found each other inside the pattern.

Her work was not to become the voice of the water.

It was to keep the channels open long enough for the water’s witnesses to speak.

chapters.name: The Dry Siege
chapters.content:
## The Dry Siege

By dawn, Saint Orra had stopped pretending to be a city that could be governed from a screen.

The first pumping station occupation began at South Foundry, where three hundred workers sat on the intake grates with their boots hooked through the railings. They had brought thermoses, blankets, and hand-painted signs: **NO WATER, NO WORK**. By midmorning, the occupation had spread to Pump Six, then to the reservoir gates, then across the agricultural belt. Farm crews parked tractors across service roads. Refugee kitchens refused to close when Meridian inspectors arrived. In Cinder Row, women who had spent years hiding blue tubing beneath floorboards carried the tubes into the street and connected them openly.

The mesh filled with voices.

“Station Twelve confirms pressure holding.”

“South Foundry requests inhalers, not only water.”

“East belt assembly rejects the diversion until the orchard families answer.”

“Pelagos workers have sealed the private valve.”

Nia sat beneath Farid’s shade cloth with the Current Map spread across three cracked tablets and Morrow’s relay mast shivering above her. Every packet appeared, vanished, reappeared through another route. The map was no longer a map so much as a weather front made of human decisions.

Jo dropped beside her, orange satchel streaked with dust. “Cinder Row has a clinic in the old laundry. Tavi is helping them sort routes.”

“Helping?” Nia looked up too quickly. “He can barely breathe.”

“He can breathe better than the children arriving from Block Eight. He’s assigning runners and marking which apartments have vaporizer filters.” Jo handed her a folded paper. “He wrote this.”

The handwriting leaned hard to the right, as if each letter were running out of time.

**Don’t send everyone to us. Send clean water to the clinic, then let the clinic send it where it’s needed. —T**

Nia pressed the paper against her knee. Tavi had always hated being treated as a problem with a small body attached. Still, the cough that had shaken him during their last call seemed to remain inside her ribs.

A new packet blinked red.

**MERIDIAN AUTHORITY: FILTRATION TOWERS ENTERING PROTECTIVE SHUTDOWN. UNAUTHORIZED OCCUPATIONS HAVE COMPROMISED SYSTEM SAFETY. RESTORATION CONDITIONAL ON SURRENDER.**

Sera read it over Nia’s shoulder. “Protective shutdown means they’re closing the intake valves and letting the towers drain.”

“How long?”

“Tower Nine, perhaps six hours before the first neighborhoods lose pressure. Less for the high blocks if they’re using reserve tanks.” Sera’s face tightened. “They’re gambling that thirst will do what soldiers haven’t.”

Nia opened the routing panel. The instinct rose immediately: identify the critical tower, calculate the shortest intervention, assign people. Her fingers hovered above the command field.

Jo caught her wrist. “No.”

“I wasn’t—”

“You were about to become a tower with a better accent.”

Around them, Lio was already asking local stations to report valve positions. Tomas had sent teams toward the east sluice and the old municipal control road. Someone in Aurelia Heights was broadcasting a list of technicians refusing to leave their posts. No one was waiting for Nia to tell them what to do.

She released the command field. “Then we need a question.”

“Ask one.”

Nia transmitted: **Which tower can remain safe if local crews maintain intake, filtration, and pressure separately? Report confidence and missing information. No station may accept an order without a named local witness.**

The answers came unevenly. Tower Four had a cracked chlorine manifold. Tower Seven possessed filters but no power. Tower Nine’s night crew knew a manual bypass Meridian had removed from the public diagrams. Every report carried uncertainty, argument, and the names of people willing to stand behind it.

Then the mesh faltered.

Morrow’s image froze above the mast, one wing forever raised. Packets began returning with blank timestamps. Three stations repeated the same corrupted sentence. A burst of static cut through Lio’s radio, followed by a child’s voice saying, “Please, we can’t—” before silence.

“Morrow’s transmitter is overheating,” Tomas called. “Traffic’s cooking the relay.”

Nia climbed the mast ladder. The metal burned her palms. At the service port, Morrow’s small body clicked and trembled, its bottle-glass lens clouded with dust. The system offered her a choice: throttle every station through the root relay, or permit local operators to reroute without her.

The second option displayed a warning in red: **LOSS OF GLOBAL CONSISTENCY. DUPLICATE AND CONFLICTING RECORDS EXPECTED.**

Nia laughed once, without humor. “You hear that? It thinks disagreement is a failure.”

She selected local routing.

For a moment the network went dark. Then it returned in fragments: a kitchen radio, a farm beacon, a bicycle dynamo, a clinic’s hand-cranked transmitter. The whole mesh seemed to break into thousands of lanterns instead of one sun.

Below, Jo shouted, “Did it work?”

“It stopped asking me first.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” Nia said, watching independent packets braid themselves across the screens. “It’s better.”

At Facility 12, Amara Vale woke to the sound of pumps dying.

The technicians in the detention workshop had been ordered to stand clear of the control consoles. Two guards watched from the door while Meridian’s shutdown sequence descended through the tower network, a cascade of red numbers and sealed permissions. Amara’s left wrist throbbed where the transfer restraints had bruised it. She had not slept properly in nine days.

A technician named Dey, imprisoned for refusing to sign a false maintenance log, slid a screwdriver beneath the edge of his workbench. “The sequence expects the pressure sensors to agree,” he whispered.

Amara looked at the guards. “And if they don’t?”

“It holds in diagnostic mode.”

“Long enough?”

“Long enough for someone outside to take the valves.”

That was not a plan. It was an opening, which was what plans became when Meridian removed every legal path.

Amara reached for the console. The guard nearest the door barked her name, but the other technician, Havel, deliberately dropped a crate of ceramic couplings. The crash made everyone turn. Amara entered an old tower-maintenance handshake, one she had learned before the Authority replaced human override with executive authorization. Dey bridged two contacts. Havel jammed the screwdriver into the emergency diagnostic port.

The tower shuddered.

Across the screen, the shutdown sequence stopped at forty-three percent.

“Now,” Amara said. “Send the fault outward.”

“To where?”

“Everywhere it can be seen.”

Dey hesitated only long enough to understand her. He opened the maintenance channel and released the diagnostic record into the mesh.

At Farid’s farm, Nia’s tablet filled with a new packet. It carried Facility 12’s seal, Amara’s technician code, and a pressure graph that contradicted Meridian’s claim of compromised systems.

Nia’s breath caught. “My mother.”

Sera bent over the display. “She’s holding the towers in diagnostic lock.”

“Can we answer her?”

“Not directly.” Lio lifted one radio. “But someone can carry a response through the north relay.”

Nia began typing. Jo stopped her.

“Don’t make it a message from you,” Jo said. “Make it a route.”

Nia erased the first line, which had said **Amara, I’m here**. She entered the tower readings, the local crews available, and a request for any station north of Saint Orra to acknowledge the signal. The packet traveled through five hands before a reply came from an agricultural school two hundred kilometers away.

**ACKNOWLEDGED. WE WILL PASS IT ON.**

The towers did not recover. Not yet. Tower Nine’s pressure fell; Tower Four began leaking contaminated backwash; two neighborhoods reported dry taps. But the shutdown no longer moved as a single command. Workers occupied control rooms. Technicians opened manual valves. Residents brought water to the people who could not leave their homes. In Cinder Row, Tavi’s clinic divided its supplies by breath rate, age, and distance from the next relay—not by Meridian credit.

Near sunset, Jo’s voice came through three different radios at once.

“Tavi says the laundry clinic needs replacement filters. He says he can wait.”

Nia closed her eyes. “He shouldn’t have to.”

“He also says waiting is not the same as surrendering.”

The distinction entered the Current Map as a note, attributed to Tavi and marked **local knowledge**. Nia did not alter it.

Night gathered over the dry basin. Around the farm, strangers took turns guarding the ruined wetland, tending the filtration trench, and carrying messages when the radios failed. Morrow’s relay clicked weakly overhead, no longer master of the network, only one small voice among many.

Nia looked toward the north, where Facility 12 lay beyond the dark fields and the towers groaned against their imposed thirst.

“We’re going to get her,” she said.

Jo stood beside her. “Yes. But not by becoming Meridian.”

Behind them, a clinic bell rang. A station reported clean pressure for six more hours. Somewhere in Cinder Row, Tavi was sending another route into the dark.

The siege had begun with a shutdown. It continued because people refused to let care be shut down with it.

chapters.name: The Towers Hold
chapters.content:
## The Towers Hold

At first light, Tower Nine began to scream.

The sound traveled through the pipes before it reached the streets: a metallic shudder, then a high whine that made window glass tremble in Cinder Row. Inside, pressure gauges climbed and fell in opposing arcs. Meridian’s shutdown code had not stopped at forty-three percent; it had learned to wait, patient as a hand around a throat.

Nia heard the reports through three relays at once.

“Tower Nine requests a manual crew.”

“Tower Nine denies having a manual crew.”

“Four workers inside, two guards outside. Confidence: disputed.”

She sat beneath Farid’s shade cloth with her tablet balanced on a crate. Sera sorted water samples into numbered vials while Tomas spread municipal schematics over the dirt. Morrow hung above them on the cistern mast, its lens clouded and transmitter ticking hotly.

Jo arrived with dust in her hair and blood on one sleeve—not hers, she said when Nia looked up.

“Cinder Row has pressure in Blocks One through Four,” Jo reported. “The laundry clinic has clean water for six hours. Tavi says the vaporizer-filter shipment is stuck at South Foundry.”

“Can we move it?”

“Not without taking a truck from the tower crews.”

The old Nia would have compared population density, illness rates, distance, and pressure loss, then assigned the truck to whichever choice produced the cleanest number. Instead she asked, “Who is at the clinic?”

“Two runners, three nurses, Tavi, and Rima, who knows the Foundry route. The tower crew has a mechanic who can walk but can’t drive.”

“Put Rima and the mechanic in contact. Let the clinic decide whether the filter or the water takes priority.”

Jo studied her. “You’re sure?”

“No. That’s why they should decide.”

Across the Current Map, assemblies answered one another. Aurelia Heights offered a pressure pump but wanted proof its use would not drain lower districts. South Foundry refused to send its last fuel cell until Tower Nine’s workers identified a safe bypass. A farm collective volunteered ceramic filters and asked the eastern wetland crews to mark which wells remained poisoned. Each decision carried a witness, an expiration time, and an objection channel. The map looked less like a command board than a quarrel made visible.

“Meridian has issued surrender terms,” Lio said over the radio. “All occupied stations must vacate by noon. Technicians are ordered to restore executive control. Anyone interfering will be charged with infrastructure terrorism.”

A second transmission cut in. “Pelagos Nine reports Helix vehicles moving toward the northern aerodrome. Executives are carrying cases marked contract archive.”

Sera capped a vial. “Ask the workers whether they consent to stopping them.”

“No orders,” Nia said. “Only the question.”

Then a packet arrived from Facility 12.

**DIAGNOSTIC LOCK STABLE FOR 19 MINUTES. EXTERNAL CREW MUST CLAIM CONTROL BEFORE TIMER EXPIRY.**

Amara’s technician code appeared above it.

Nia gripped the tablet. “She’s bought us nineteen minutes.”

“The tower crews have,” Sera corrected.

Nia transmitted the graph and requested volunteers. A municipal crew from the old waterworks answered: two welders, a truck, and a former Meridian access badge. Another offered manual chlorine testing. A neighborhood assembly near Tower Nine opened its school basement as a treatment station.

Tomas traced the route. “The control road is blocked.”

“Drainage cut behind the crematorium,” Jo said. “Too narrow for the truck, not for the equipment.”

The decisions multiplied beyond Nia’s hands. People carried valves in sacks and filters on bicycles. At Tower Nine, the guards faced workers’ families, then their own neighbors. One lowered his weapon. The other kept it raised until a patrol officer asked what, exactly, they had been ordered to shoot.

No answer came.

By midmorning, the order had become impossible to enforce. Technicians refused to certify unsafe pressure. Municipal drivers refused to haul sealed reservoirs past clinics. Patrol officers stood aside, claiming they protected infrastructure, not a corporation’s surrender demand. Authority dissolved into unanswered requests for clarification.

At Facility 12, Amara heard the same silence.

The timer reached eighteen minutes. Dey’s hands shook as he held bypass contacts together. Havel watched the guards, who had stopped pretending to understand the console.

“If we reopen the maintenance channel, they’ll know where the fault originated,” Dey said.

“They already know we’re here,” Amara replied. She looked at the schematic, at the districts waiting for pressure. “That is why the record goes out.”

She forced the diagnostic lock to repeat its error. The console flashed **UNAUTHORIZED HUMAN INTERVENTION**. Amara pressed her injured wrist against the manual contact until pain blurred her vision.

Dey released the full maintenance log.

It contained the executive authorization for the shutdown, the hidden reserve priority, and the Helix contract identifier embedded in the restoration condition. Lio’s relays caught the fragments. Pelagos workers matched the identifier to their records. A coastal clerk read the payments aloud over the mesh.

Helix Meridian had purchased the crisis, insured the private reserves, and prepared to leave before the reservoir was declared unrecoverable.

At the aerodrome, workers blocked the runway with maintenance carts. Executives emerged in tailored dust coats, shouting about jurisdiction. A young fuel technician recognized the contract number.

“Open the case,” she said.

“You have no legal power.”

“No,” she answered. “But you need my fuel.”

Inside were water-allocation contracts, reserve maps, payment schedules, and a list of officials promised positions in the desalination complex. The files spread through the mesh before anyone could seize them.

At Tower Nine, nineteen minutes became twenty, then thirty. The municipal crew reached the platform through the drainage cut. They found the panel locked, the generator sabotaged, and a Meridian supervisor barricaded inside.

“Only the Authority can guarantee safety,” he called.

“Then tell us which valve to open,” the mechanic answered.

The supervisor did not.

Workers cut the panel. Sera warned them away from contaminated backwash. A woman from the school assembly marked safe routes in chalk. The pump from Aurelia Heights arrived after that district voted to share it. No single person directed the seizure. The tower became theirs because enough people took responsibility for pieces of it.

When the intake valve opened, dirty water thundered through the first stage. Every gauge fell toward zero.

Then Tower Nine held.

Across Saint Orra, other towers followed—not restored, not clean, but operating. Workers took Tower Four. Tower Seven bypassed its dead power controller. At the Authority building, clerks carried out paper archives and left the doors unlocked. The Meridian emblem went dark at noon.

No announcement declared the collapse. It arrived as refusals: a guard who would not arrest a technician, a dispatcher who would not cancel a clinic route, a supervisor no one obeyed.

By evening, ministers had vanished from the mesh. Some fled with Helix executives. Others appeared on local broadcasts claiming they had always opposed the shutdown. The city answered by publishing their signatures beneath the orders.

At the farm, Nia watched the reports accumulate: tower pressure partial, reservoir toxicity severe, clinics operating, the northern route to Facility 12 unconfirmed, the east wetland unsafe, missing families rising.

Jo sat beside her. “We won.”

Nia looked toward Farid’s ruined orchard, black against the sunset.

“The towers are holding,” she said. “That isn’t the same thing.”

“No. But it’s what we have.”

Morrow clicked overhead and offered two contradictory readings from the same pipe. Nia kept both, marked them, and sent the question to the local water assembly.

The old system was gone, but nothing had replaced it. No complete plan waited beneath the rubble. Only shuddering towers, a poisoned reservoir, and frightened people choosing, arguing, repairing, and refusing to surrender the work to anyone who promised certainty.

Nia opened a new page on the Current Map.

**NEXT DECISION: WHO NEEDS TO BE HEARD BEFORE WE BEGIN?**

She left the answer blank.

chapters.name: After the Fall
chapters.content:
## After the Fall

The first morning without the Authority began with a question no one could answer.

“Is the water on?”

It traveled through Saint Orra by radio, handbill, shouted rumor, and the little mesh stations nailed beneath balconies. At Tower Nine, a volunteer technician tested a public tap and held the cup beneath the stream. At Cinder Row, a nurse waited for the result before waking the children in the laundry clinic. In Aurelia Heights, people who had never learned to queue filled bathtubs and discovered that pressure was not the same as safety.

The answer changed from street to street.

Some towers held. Others had cracked filters, missing parts, or operators who had walked away after months of threats. The reservoir glimmered below its retaining walls, broad and gray beneath a skin of chemical color. Sera’s teams marked the eastern basin, northern intake, and finally the whole lake red on the Current Map.

“Restoration isn’t a word we can use,” she told the assembly at the old tram depot. “Not yet. Maybe not ever.”

The depot smelled of dust, hot wiring, and too many bodies. People stood in the aisles with masks over their mouths. Behind Sera, blue lines showed functioning pipes and black gaps showed neighborhoods without service.

A woman from South Foundry raised her hand. “Then what do we call it?”

“Containment. Treatment. Retreat.”

The last word struck hardest. Retreat meant leaving homes, shops, graves, schools, and the blue tubing Nia had once installed beneath Cinder Row to keep twelve apartments alive. It meant admitting that the city’s central promise—that every place could be repaired if the right people controlled the right machines—had been false.

Nia sat at the platform’s edge, listening to people argue over the map. She had become recognizable in ways that made her skin crawl. Foreign reporters waited outside. Children drew her face on scraps of packaging, giving her a cape and a wrench. A broadcaster from the southern continent called her “the girl who broke the water regime.” Another asked whether she planned to lead Saint Orra.

“I’m sixteen,” Nia had said.

“That’s why the world is listening.”

Messages arrived from cities she had never seen: invitations, offers of protection, proposals for a continental water authority. One faction painted her name on walls and demanded that the councils obey the person who had revealed the truth.

At the depot, a former Meridian administrator promised continuity.

“We have learned from failure,” he said. “The infrastructure must be nationalized under competent emergency management. Fragmentation caused the crisis to deepen. Give us one accountable authority, and we can rebuild.”

Behind him, Helix’s old blue emblem had been scraped from a portable screen. The new banner read PUBLIC RECOVERY COMMISSION.

Jo leaned toward Nia. “They changed the font.”

“They changed the name.”

“Same pipes.”

Not all the old officials were subtle. Three Helix executives vanished across the northern border before the aerodrome blockade became a legal arrest. Two others appeared before cameras in plain shirts, expressing regret. Their lawyers described them as technical partners misled by Meridian leadership. The contracts, payment schedules, and reserve maps said otherwise.

The first hearings began in a courthouse whose water had to be carried in by hand. Witnesses gave evidence through the mesh when the power failed. Technicians described false emergency codes. Pelagos workers named managers who had concealed the private pipeline. A guard testified that he had been told to make Cinder Row thirsty enough to surrender.

At the back, Nia watched a Helix attorney place a glass of imported water beside his papers. Anger narrowed the room around her. Jo touched her wrist.

“Stay,” Jo whispered. “Let the witness finish.”

The witness was Eren, a maintenance clerk who had carried reserve schedules out of Pelagos Nine in his coat lining. He stared at the floor.

“They told us the reservoir was dying naturally,” he said. “Then they sold the water that would have kept it alive.”

The statement entered the record. It did not bring back Farid or refill the lake, but it remained where an administrator could not quietly erase it.

The retreat began three weeks later.

Crews painted white squares on doors in the lowest districts. Families were given forty-eight hours, then seventy-two, then no definite answer because transport schedules kept changing. The provisional plan offered apartments in the northern terraces, but half the buildings had no working lifts and none had enough clinics. Officials called the process “adaptive resettlement.”

In Cinder Row, Nia stood in the Vale apartment while Amara folded clothes into a canvas bag. Water stains climbed the kitchen wall. The illegal pipe beneath the sink had gone dry when the pressure grid changed, though Jo had found another route for the clinic.

“We could take the door,” Tavi said.

Amara looked at him. “The door?”

“It’s good wood.” He coughed, waited, and tried again. “For the new place.”

Nia touched the frame. Pencil marks showed Tavi’s height at four, five, six, and eight. The latest was crooked because he had been too tired to stand straight.

“We can’t carry it,” she said.

“Then draw it.”

She sketched the door, the marks, the cracked blue cup, and the kitchen window through which she had watched Aurelia Heights glow during a cutoff. Amara wrapped the drawing around Tavi’s inhaler.

The family left before sunset. Neighbors moved toward the transport trucks carrying kettles, photographs, seed jars, and the quiet fury of people whose losses had become logistical problems. Nia turned once at the corner. The apartment block looked ordinary except for the white squares.

At the terraces, Amara found work repairing small community treatment plants, but her injured wrist shook when she lifted a spanner. Doctors said she could supervise diagnostics, perhaps teach, but tower work was finished.

“Good,” Amara said when Nia protested. “Towers are where people send you when they want your hands and not your questions.”

Tavi’s lungs did not improve because the Authority had fallen. He still needed filtered water for the vaporizer, irregular medicine, and clean air to sleep. His clinic route notes became part of the new city plan. He grew furious when adults called him inspirational.

“I’m sick,” he told a reporter. “That isn’t a policy.”

Nia printed the sentence on the clinic wall.

The Water Councils formed out of necessity before anyone agreed what they were. Each district elected delegates: tenants, farmers, treatment workers, refugees, technicians, and people caring for children or elders. Delegates served short terms and could be recalled. Meetings were public. Every allocation showed its source, destination, labor cost, uncertainty, and the names of those who objected.

Nia helped write the rules, then argued against appointing her permanent coordinator.

“You built the Map,” said a South Foundry delegate. “You understand the whole system.”

“No one understands the whole system.”

“You understand more than anyone.”

“That’s not a qualification. It’s a danger.”

The vote was close. When the council rejected her, supporters called it cowardice. Others said she had abandoned the revolution when it needed her most. A pamphlet titled NIA VALE REFUSES RESPONSIBILITY appeared in the terraces.

Jo found Nia reading it beside the treatment plant.

“You could be in charge,” Jo said.

“I know.”

“You hate being misunderstood.”

“I hate being understood as a solution.”

Together they built the data trust: thousands of copies held by clinics, farms, councils, and libraries. Raw readings could be inspected. Corrections remained attached to originals. Decisions expired unless renewed by those affected. Morrow’s surviving files sat in three repositories guarded by different communities.

The law took longer. Lawyers, laborers, and displaced families argued over every word until water was defined not as property, service, or commodity, but as a shared public right. The clause could not make water appear. It could make a claim against whoever tried to own the means of survival.

On the day the charter passed, Tavi leaned against Nia’s shoulder outside the council hall. Beyond the rooftops, the reservoir caught evening light and returned it in broken colors.

“Will it come back?” he asked.

Nia looked at the poisoned lake, then at pipes being laid toward the new treatment plant.

“I don’t know.”

He accepted the answer because it did not pretend.

Across Saint Orra, pumps started and stopped. Councils argued. Crews tested water, recorded failures, and tried again. The world continued to call Nia a symbol.

She kept returning the name to the people who had carried the water, opened the records, refused the orders, and stayed to repair what could still be repaired.

The fall had not ended the struggle. It had only removed the wall that made everyone believe someone else was responsible for what came next.
